speaker: KERRY
sentence: Yes, I do.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But before I answer further, let me thank you for moderating.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I want to thank the University of Miami for hosting us.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I know the President will join me in welcoming all of Florida to this debate.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You've been through the roughest weeks anybody could imagine.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Our hearts go out to you, and we admire your pluck and perseverance.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I can make America safer than President Bush has made us.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I believe President Bush and I both love our country equally, but we just have a different set of convictions about how you make America safe.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe America is safest and strongest when we are leading the world and when we are leading strong alliances.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'll never give a veto to any country over our security, but I also know how to lead those alliances.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This President has left them in shatters across the globe, and we're now 90 percent of the casualties in Iraq and 90 percent of the costs.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think that's wrong, and I think we can do better.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I have a better plan for homeland security.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I have a better plan to be able to fight the war on terror: by strengthening our military; strengthening our intelligence; by going after the financing more authoritatively; by doing what we need to do to rebuild the alliances; by reaching out to the Muslim world, which the President has almost not done; and beginning to isolate the radical Islamic Muslims, not have them isolate the United States of America.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I know I can do a better job in Iraq, where I have a plan to have a summit with all of the allies, something this President has not yet achieved, not yet been able to do to bring people to the table.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We can do a better job of training the Iraqi forces to defend themselves.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I know that we can do a better job of preparing for elections.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: All of these, and especially homeland security, which we'll talk about a little bit later.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I too thank the University of Miami and say our prayers are with the good people of this State who've suffered a lot.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: September the 11th changed how America must look at the world.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And since that day, our Nation has been on a multipronged strategy to keep our country safer.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've pursued Al Qaida wherever Al Qaida tries to hide; 75 percent of known Al Qaida leaders have been brought to justice.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The rest of them know we're after them.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've upheld the doctrine that said, "If you harbor a terrorist, you're equally as guilty as the terrorist." And the Taliban, no longer in power; 10 million people have registered to vote in Afghanistan in the upcoming Presidential election.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: In Iraq, we saw a threat, and we realized that after September the 11th, we must take threats seriously before they fully materialize.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Saddam Hussein now sits in a prison cell.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: America and the world are safer for it.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We continue to pursue our policy of disrupting those who proliferate weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Libya has disarmed.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The A.Q.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Khan network has been brought to justice.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And as well, we're pursuing a strategy of—of freedom around the world, because I understand free nations will reject terror; free nations will answer the hopes and aspirations of their people; free nations will help us achieve the peace we all want.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: No, I don't believe it's going to happen.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I believe I'm going to win because the American people know I know how to lead.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I've shown the American people I know how to lead.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I have—I understand everybody in this country doesn't agree with the decisions that I've made, and I made some tough decisions.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But people know where I stand.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: People out there listening know what I believe, and that's how best it is to keep the peace.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: This Nation of ours has got a solemn duty to defeat this ideology of hate, and that's what they are.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: This is a group of killers who will not only kill here but kill children in Russia, that will attack unmercifully in Iraq hoping to shake our will.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We have a duty to defeat this enemy.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We have a duty to protect our children and grandchildren.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The best way to defeat them is to never waver, to be strong, to use every asset at our disposal, is to constantly stay on the offensive, and at the same time, spread liberty.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And that's what people are seeing now is happening in Afghanistan.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Ten million citizens have registered to vote.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's a phenomenal statistic, that if given a chance to be free, they will show up at the polls.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Forty-one percent of those 10 million are women.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: In Iraq, no doubt about it, it's tough.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's hard work.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's incredibly hard.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You know why?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Because an enemy realizes the stakes.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The enemy understands a free Iraq will be a major defeat in their ideology of hatred.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's why they're fighting so vociferously.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: They showed up in Afghanistan when they were there because they tried to beat us, and they didn't.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And they're showing up in Iraq for the same reason.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: They're trying to defeat us.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And if we lose our will, we lose.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But if we remain strong and resolute, we will defeat this enemy.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe in being strong and resolute and determined, and I will hunt down and kill the terrorists, wherever they are.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But we also have to be smart, Jim, and smart means not diverting your attention from the real war on terror in Afghanistan against Usama bin Laden and taking it off to Iraq, where the 9/11 Commission confirms there was no connection to 9/11 itself and Saddam Hussein, and where the reason for going to war was weapons of mass destruction, not the removal of Saddam Hussein.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This President has made, I regret to say, a colossal error of judgment.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And judgment is what we look for in the President of the United States of America.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm proud that important military figures are supporting me in this race: former Chairman of Joint Chiefs of Staff John Shalikashvili; just yesterday General Eisenhower's son, General John Eisenhower, endorsed me; General—Admiral William Crowe; General Tony McPeak, who ran the Air Force war so effectively for his father.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: All believe I would make a stronger Commander in Chief.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And they believe it because they know I would not take my eye off of the goal, Usama bin Laden.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Unfortunately, he escaped in the mountains of Tora Bora.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We had him surrounded.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But we didn't use American forces, the best trained in the world, to go kill him.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President relied on Afghan warlords that he outsourced that job to.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's wrong.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, where do you want me to begin?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: First of all, he made the misjudgment of saying to America that he was going to build a true alliance, that he would exhaust the remedies of the United Nations and go through the inspections.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: In fact, he first didn't even want to do that, and it wasn't until former Secretary of State Jim Baker and General Scowcroft and others pushed publicly and said, "You've got to go to the U.N.," that the President finally changed his mind— his campaign has a word for that—and went to the United Nations.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, once there, we could have continued those inspections.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We had Saddam Hussein trapped.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: He also promised America that he would go to war as a last resort.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Those words mean something to me, as somebody who has been in combat, "last resort." You've got to be able to look in the eyes of families and say to those parents, "I tried to do everything in my power to prevent the loss of your son and daughter." I don't believe the United States did that, and we pushed our allies aside.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And so today, we are 90 percent of the casualties and 90 percent of the cost, $200 billion—$200 billion that could have been used for health care, for schools, for construction, for prescription drugs for seniors, and it's in Iraq.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And Iraq is not even the center of the focus of the war on terror.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The center is Afghanistan where, incidentally, there were more Americans killed last year than the year before, where the opium production is 75 percent of the world's opium production, where 40 to 60 percent of the economy of Afghanistan is based on opium, where the elections have been postponed 3 times.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President moved the troops, so he's got 10 times the number of troops in Iraq than he has in Afghanistan, where Usama bin Laden is.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Does that mean that Saddam Hussein was 10 times more important than Usama bin Laden— excuse me—Saddam Hussein more important than Usama bin Laden?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I don't think so.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent looked at the same intelligence I looked at and declared, in 2002, that Saddam Hussein was a grave threat.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He also said, in December of 2003, that anyone who doubts that the world is safer without Saddam Hussein does not have the judgment to be President.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I agree with him.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The world is better off without Saddam Hussein.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I was hoping diplomacy would work.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I understand the serious consequences of committing our troops into harm's way.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's the hardest decision a President makes.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: So I went to the United Nations.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I didn't need anybody to tell me to go to the United Nations; I decided to go there myself.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And I went there hoping that, once and for all, the free world would act in concert to get Saddam Hussein to listen to our demands.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And they passed a resolution that said, "Disclose, disarm, or face serious consequences." I believe when an international body speaks, it must mean what it says.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But Saddam Hussein had no intention of disarming.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Why should he?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He had 16 other resolutions, and nothing took place.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: As a matter of fact—my opponent talks about inspectors—the facts are that he was systematically deceiving the inspectors.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That wasn't going to work.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's kind of a pre-September-10th mentality, to hope that somehow resolutions and failed inspections would make this world a more peaceful place.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He was hoping we'd turn away.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But there was, fortunately, others beside myself who believed that we ought to take action, and we did.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The world is safer without Saddam Hussein.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Jim, we've got the capability of doing both.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: As a matter of fact, this is a global effort.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're facing a— a group of folks who have such hatred in their heart, they'll strike anywhere with any means.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And that's why it's essential that we have strong alliances, and we do.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's why it's essential that we make sure that we keep weapons of mass destruction out of the hands of people like Al Qaida, which we are.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But to say that there's only one focus on the war on terror doesn't really understand the nature of the war on terror.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Of course we're after Saddam Hussein— I mean, bin Laden.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He's—he's isolated.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Seventy-five percent of his people have been brought to justice.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The killer in—the mastermind of the September the 11th attacks, Khalid Sheik Mohammad, is in prison.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're making progress, but the front on this war is more than just one place.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The Philippines—we've got help—we're helping them there to bring—to bring Al Qaida affiliates to justice there.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And of course Iraq is a central part of the war on terror.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's why Zarqawi and his people are trying to fight us.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Their hope is that we grow weary and we leave.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The biggest disaster that could happen is that we not succeed in Iraq.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We will succeed.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've got a plan to do so, and the main reason we'll succeed is because the Iraqis want to be free.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I had the honor of visiting with Prime Minister Allawi.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He's a strong, courageous leader.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He believes in the freedom of the Iraqi people.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He doesn't want U.S.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: leadership, however, to send mixed signals, to not stand with the Iraqi people.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He believes, like I believe, that the Iraqis are ready to fight for their own freedom.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: They just need the help to be trained.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: There will be elections in January.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're spending reconstruction money.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And our alliance is strong.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's the plan for victory.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And when Iraq is free, America will be more secure.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President just talked about Iraq as a center of the war on terror.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Iraq was not even close to the center of the war on terror before the President invaded it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President made the judgment to divert forces from under General Tommy Franks from Afghanistan before the Congress even approved it, to begin to prepare to go to war in Iraq.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And he rushed to war in Iraq without a plan to win the peace.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, that is not the judgment that a President of the United States ought to make.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You don't take America to war unless you have a plan to win the peace.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You don't send troops to war without the body armor that they need.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've met kids in Ohio, parents in Wisconsin, places—Iowa, where they're going out on the Internet to get the state-of-the-art body gear to send to their kids—some of them have got them for a birthday present.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think that's wrong.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Humvees—10,000 out of 12,000 Humvees that are over there aren't armored.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And you go visit some of those kids in the hospitals today who were maimed because they don't have the armament.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This President just—I don't know if he sees what's really happening out there, but it's getting worse by the day—more soldiers killed in June than before, more in July than June, more in August than July, more in September than in August.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And now we see beheadings, and we've got weapons of mass destruction crossing the border every single day, and they're blowing people up.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And we don't have enough troops there.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Can I respond?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Thank you, sir.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: First of all, what my opponent wants you to forget is that he voted to authorize the use of force and now says, "It's the wrong war at the wrong time at the wrong place." I don't see how you can lead this country to succeed in Iraq if you say "wrong war, wrong time, wrong place." What message does that send our troops?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: What message does that send our allies?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: What message does that send the Iraqis?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: No, the way to win this is to be steadfast and resolved and to follow through on the plan that I've just outlined.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Yes, we have to be steadfast and resolved, and I am.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I will succeed for those troops, now that we're there.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We have to succeed.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We can't leave a failed Iraq.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But that doesn't mean it wasn't a mistake of judgment to go there and take the focus off of Usama bin Laden.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It was.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, we can succeed, but I don't believe this President can.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think we need a President who has the credibility to bring the allies back to the table and to do what's necessary to make it so America isn't doing this alone.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Jim, let me tell you exactly what I'll do, and there are a long list of things.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: First of all, what kind of mixed message does it send when you've got $500 million going over to Iraq to put police officers in the streets of Iraq and the President is cutting the COPS program in America?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: What kind of message does it send to be sending money to open firehouses in Iraq, but we're shutting firehouses, who are the first-responders, here in America?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President hasn't put one nickel— not one nickel—into the effort to fix some of our tunnels and bridges and most exposed subway systems.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's why they had to close down the subway in New York when the Republican Convention was there.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We hadn't done the work that ought to be done.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President—95 percent of the containers that come into the ports, right here in Florida, are not inspected.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Civilians get onto aircraft, and their—their luggage is X-rayed, but the cargo hold is not X-rayed.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Does that make you feel safer in America?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This President thought it was more important to give the wealthiest people in America a tax cut rather than invest in homeland security.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Those aren't my values.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe in protecting America first.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And long before President Bush and I get a tax cut—and that's who gets it—long before we do, I'm going to invest in homeland security, and I'm going to make sure we're not cutting COPS programs in America, and we're fully staffed at our firehouses and that we protect the nuclear and chemical plants.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President also, unfortunately, gave in to the chemical industry, which didn't want to do some of the things necessary to strengthen our chemical plant exposure.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And there's an enormous undone job to protect the loose nuclear materials in the world that are able to get to terrorists.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's a whole other subject, but—I see we still have a little bit more time.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Let me just quickly say, at the current pace the President will not secure the loose material in the Soviet Union—former Soviet Union for 13 years.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm going to do it in 4 years.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And we're going to keep it out of the hands of terrorists.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I don't think we want to get to how he's going to pay for all these promises.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's like a huge tax gap and—anyway, that's for another debate.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My administration has tripled the amount of money we're spending on homeland security, to $30 billion a year.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My administration worked with the Congress to create the Department of Homeland Security so we could better coordinate our borders and ports.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've got 1,000 extra Border Patrol on the southern border, more than 1,000 on the northern border.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're modernizing our borders.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've spent $3.1 billion for fire and police—$3.1 billion.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're doing our duty to provide the funding.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But the best way to protect this homeland is to stay on the offense.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We have to be right 100 percent of the time, and the enemy only has to be right once to hurt us.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: There's a lot of good people working hard.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And by the way, we've also changed the culture of the FBI to have counterterrorism as its number one priority.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're communicating better.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're going to reform our intelligence services to make sure that we get the best intelligence possible.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The PATRIOT Act is vital.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's vital that the Congress renew the PATRIOT Act, which enables our law enforcement to disrupt terrorist cells.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But again, I repeat to my fellow citizens, the best way to protect you is to stay on the offense.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President just said the FBI had changed its culture.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We just read on the front pages of America's papers that there are over 100,000 hours of tapes unlistened to.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: On one of those tapes may be the enemy being right the next time.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And the test is not whether you're spending more money.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The test is, are you doing everything possible to make America safe?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We didn't need that tax cut.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: America needed to be safe.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Of course we're doing everything we can to protect America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I wake up every day thinking about how best to protect America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's my job.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I work with Director Mueller of the FBI.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He comes into my office, when I'm in Washington, every morning talking about how to protect us.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: There's a lot of really good people working hard to do so.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's hard work.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But again, I want to tell the American people, we're doing everything we can at home, but you better have a President who chases these terrorists down and bring them to justice before they hurt us again.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Let me first tell you that the best way for Iraq to be safe and secure is for Iraqi citizens to be trained to do the job.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And that's what we're doing.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We got 100,000 trained now, 125,000 by the end of this year, over 200,000 by the end of next year.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That is the best way.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We'll never succeed in Iraq if the Iraqi citizens do not want to take matters into their own hands and protect themselves.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I believe they want to.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Prime Minister Allawi believes they want to.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so the best indication about when we can bring our troops home—which I really want to do, but I don't want to do so for the sake of bringing them home; I want to do so because we've achieved an objective—is to see the Iraqis perform, is to see the Iraqis step up and take responsibility.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so the answer to your question is, when our generals on the ground and Ambassador Negroponte tells me that Iraq is ready to defend herself from these terrorists, that elections will have been held by then, that there's stability, and that they're on their way to—you know, a nation of— that's free.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's when.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And I hope it's as soon as possible.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But I know putting artificial deadlines won't work.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent one time said, "Well, get me elected, I'll have them out of there in 6 months." That's—you can't do that and expect to win the war on terror.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My message to our troops is: Thank you for what you're doing; we're standing with you strong; we'll give you all the equipment you need; and we'll get you home as soon as the mission's done, because this is a vital mission.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: A free Iraq will be a ally in the war on terror, and that's essential.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: A free Iraq will set a powerful example in the part of the world that is desperate for freedom.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: A free Iraq will help secure Israel.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: A free Iraq will enforce the hopes and aspirations of the reformers in places like Iran.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: A free Iraq is essential for the security of this country.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Thank you, Jim.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: My message to the troops is also "Thank you" for what they're doing, but it's also, "Help is on the way." I believe those troops deserve better than what they are getting today.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You know, it's interesting, when I was in the ropeline just the other day coming out here from Wisconsin, a couple of young returnees were in the line, one active duty, one from the Guard.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And they both looked at me and said, "We need you.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You've got to help us over there." Now, I believe there's a better way to do this.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You know, the President's father did not go into Iraq—into Baghdad, beyond Basra.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And the reason he didn't is, he said—he wrote in his book, because there was no viable exit strategy.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And he said our troops would be occupiers in a bitterly hostile land.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's exactly where we find ourselves today.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: There's a sense of American occupation.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The only building that was guarded when the troops went into Baghdad was the oil ministry.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We didn't guard the nuclear facilities.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We didn't guard the foreign office, where you might have found information about weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We didn't guard the borders.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Almost every step of the way, our troops have been left on these extraordinarily difficult missions.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I know what it's like to go out on one of those missions where you don't know what's around the corner.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I believe our troops need other allies helping.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm going to hold that summit.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I will bring fresh credibility, a new start, and we will get the job done right.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Jim——

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think it's worthy for a followup——

speaker: BUSH
sentence: ——if you don't mind.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Let's change the rules.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We can add a whole— .

speaker: BUSH
sentence: All right.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent says, "Help is on the way," but what kind of message does it say to our troops in harm's way, "wrong war, wrong place, wrong time"?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's not a message a Commander in Chief gives—or "This is a great diversion." As well, help is on the way, but it's certainly hard to tell it when he voted against the $87 billion supplemental to provide equipment for our troops and then said he actually did vote for it before he voted against it.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's not what Commander in Chiefs does when you're trying to lead troops.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, you know, when I talked about the $87 billion, I made a mistake in how I talk about the war.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But the President made a mistake in invading Iraq.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Which is worse?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe that when you know something's going wrong, you make it right.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's what I learned in Vietnam.

speaker: KERRY

sentence: Libya understood that America and others will enforce doctrine, and the world is better for it.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: So to answer your question, I would hope we'd never have to.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think by acting firmly and decisively, it will mean it's less likely to—less likely we have to use force.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Jim, the President just said something extraordinarily revealing and, frankly, very important in this debate.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: In answer to your question about Iraq and sending people into Iraq, he just said, "The enemy attacked us." Saddam Hussein didn't attack us.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Usama bin Laden attacked us.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Al Qaida attacked us.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And when we had Usama bin Laden cornered in the mountains of Tora Bora, 1,000 of his cohorts with him in those mountains, with the American military forces nearby and in the field, we didn't use the best trained troops in the world to go kill the world's number one criminal and terrorist.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They outsourced the job to Afghan warlords who only a week earlier had been on the other side fighting against us, neither of whom trusted each other.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's the enemy that attacked us.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's the enemy that was allowed to walk out of those mountains.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's the enemy that is now in 60 countries with stronger recruits.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: He also said Saddam Hussein would have been stronger.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That is just factually incorrect.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Two-thirds of the country was a no-fly zone when we started this war.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We would have had sanctions.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We would have had the U.N.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: inspectors.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Saddam Hussein would have been continually weakening.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: If the President had shown the patience to go through another round of resolution, to sit down with those leaders and say, "What do you need?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: What do you need now?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: How much more will it take to get you to join us," we would be in a stronger place today.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: First, listen——

speaker: BUSH
sentence: ——of course I know Usama bin Laden attacked us.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I know that.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And secondly, to think that another round of resolutions would have caused Saddam Hussein to disarm, disclose is ludicrous, in my judgment.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It just shows a significant difference of opinion.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We tried diplomacy.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We did our best.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He was hoping to turn a blind eye, and, yes, he would have been stronger had we not dealt with him.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He had the capability of making weapons, and he would have made weapons.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Thirty-five to forty countries in the world had a greater capability of making weapons at the moment the President invaded than Saddam Hussein.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And while he has been diverted with 9 out of 10 active duty divisions of our Army either going to Iraq, coming back from Iraq, or getting ready to go, North Korea's got nuclear weapons, and the world is more dangerous.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Iran is moving towards nuclear weapons, and the world is more dangerous.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Darfur has a genocide.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The world is more dangerous.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'd have made a better choice.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President always has the right and always has had the right for preemptive strike.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That was a great doctrine throughout the cold war, and it was always one of the things we argued about with respect to arms control.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: No President, through all of American history, has ever ceded, and nor would I, the right to preempt in any way necessary to protect the United States of America.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But if and when you do it, Jim, you've got to do in a way that passes the test, that passes the global test, where your countrymen, your people, understand fully why you're doing what you're doing and you can prove to the world that you did it for legitimate reasons.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Here we have our own Secretary of State who's had to apologize to the world for the presentation he made to the United Nations.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I mean, we can remember when President Kennedy, in the Cuban missile crisis, sent his Secretary of State to Paris to meet with de Gaulle, and in the middle of the discussion to tell them about the missiles in Cuba, he said, "Here, let me show you the photos." And de Gaulle waved them off and said, "No, no, no, no.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The word of the President of the United States is good enough for me." How many leaders in the world today would respond to us, as a result of what we've done, in that way?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: So what is at test here is the credibility of the United States of America and how we lead the world.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Iran and Iraq are now more—Iran and North Korea are now more dangerous.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, whether preemption is ultimately what has to happen or not, I don't know yet.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But I'll tell you this, as President, I'll never take my eye off that ball.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've been fighting for proliferation the entire time—antiproliferation the entire time I've been in the Congress.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And we've watched this President actually turn away from some of the treaties that were on the table.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You don't help yourself with other nations when you turn away from the global warming treaty, for instance, or when you refuse to deal at length with the United Nations.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You have to earn that respect.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I think we have a lot of earning back to do.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Let me—I'm not exactly sure what you mean, "passes the global test." You take preemptive action if you pass a global test?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My attitude is you take preemptive action in order to protect the American people, that you act in order to make this country secure.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent talks about me not signing certain treaties.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But let me tell you one thing I didn't sign—and I think it shows a difference of our opinion, the difference of opinions—and that is that I wouldn't join the International Criminal Court.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: This is a body based in The Hague where unaccountable judges and prosecutors could pull our troops, our diplomats up for trial.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And I wouldn't join it.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And I understand that in certain capitals around the world that that wasn't a popular move.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But it's the right move, not to join a foreign court that could—where our people could be prosecuted.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent is for joining the International Criminal Court.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I just think trying to be popular kind of in the global sense, if it's not in our best interest, makes no sense.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I'm interested in working with other nations and do a lot of it.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But I'm not going to make decisions that I think are wrong for America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: North Korea, first—I do.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Let me say I certainly hope so.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Before I was sworn in, the policy of this Government was to have bilateral negotiations with North Korea.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And we signed an agreement with North Korea that my administration found out that was not being honored by the North Koreans.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so I decided that a better way to approach the issue was to get other nations involved, just—besides us.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And in Crawford, Texas, Jiang Zemin and I agreed that the nuclear-weapons-free North—peninsula—Korean Peninsula was in his interest and our interest and the world's interest.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so we began a new dialog with North Korea, one that included not only the United States but now China.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And China has got a lot of influence over North Korea, in some ways more than we do.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: As well we included South Korea, Japan, and Russia.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: So now there are five voices speaking to Kim Chong-il, not just one.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so if Kim Chong-il decides again to not honor an agreement, he's not only doing injustice to America, he'd be doing injustice to China as well.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And I think this will work.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's not going to work if we open up a dialog with Kim Chong-il.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's what he wants.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He wants to unravel the six-party talks—or the five—the five-nation coalition that's sending him a clear message.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: On Iran, I hope we can do the same thing, continue to work with the world to convince the Iranian mullahs to abandon their nuclear ambitions.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've worked very closely with the Foreign Ministers of France, Germany, and Great Britain, who have been the folks delivering the message to the mullahs that if you expect to be part of the world of nations, get rid of your nuclear programs.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The IAEA is involved.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: There's a special protocol recently been passed that allows for instant inspections.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I hope we can do it, and we've got a good strategy.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: With respect to Iran, the British, French, and Germans were the ones who initiated an effort—without the United States, regrettably—to begin to try to move to deter the nuclear possibilities in Iran.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe we could have done better.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think the United States should have offered the opportunity to provide the nuclear fuel, test them to see whether or not they were actually looking for it for peaceful purposes.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: If they weren't willing to work a deal, then we could have put sanctions together.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President did nothing.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: With respect to North Korea, the real story, we had inspectors and television cameras in the nuclear reactor in North Korea.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Secretary Bill Perry negotiated that under President Clinton.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And we knew where the fuel rods were, and we knew the limits on their nuclear power.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Colin Powell, our Secretary of State, announced one day that we were going to continue the dialog and work with the North Koreans.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President reversed him publicly, while the President of South Korea was here.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And the President of South Korea went back to South Korea bewildered and embarrassed because it went against his policy.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And for 2 years, this administration didn't talk at all to North Korea.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: While they didn't talk at all, the fuel rods came out.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The inspectors were kicked out.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The television cameras were kicked out.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And, today, there are four to seven nuclear weapons in the hands of North Korea.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That happened on this President's watch.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, that, I think, is one of the most serious sort of reversals or mixed messages that you could possibly send.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Right.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Both.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I want bilateral talks which put all of the issues from the Armistice of 1952, the economic issues, the human rights issues, the artillery disposal issues, the DMZ issues, and the nuclear issues on the table.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The minute we have bilateral talks, the six-party talks will unwind.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's exactly what Kim Chong-il wants.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And by the way, the breach on the agreement was not to plutonium.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The breach on the agreement is highly enriched uranium.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's what we caught him doing.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's where he was breaking the agreement.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Secondly, you said—my opponent said that he'd work to put sanctions on Iran.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've already sanctioned Iran.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We can't sanction them anymore.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: There are sanctions in place on Iran.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And finally, we were a party to the convincing—to working with Germany, France, and Great Britain to send their Foreign Ministers into Iran.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, I'll tell you exactly why not, but I first want to say something about those sanctions on Iran.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Only the United States put the sanctions on, alone, and that's exactly what I'm talking about.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: In order for the sanctions to be effective we should have been working with the British, French, and Germans and other countries.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And that's the difference between the President and me.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And there again, he sort of slid by the question.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, with respect to Darfur, yes, it is a genocide.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And months ago, many of us were pressing for action.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think the reason that we're not saying send American troops in at this point is several-fold.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Number one, we can do this through the African Union, providing we give them the logistical support.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Right now, all the President is providing is humanitarian support.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We need to do more than that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They've got to have the logistical capacity to go in and stop the killing, and that's going to require more than is on the table today.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I also believe that it is—one of the reasons we can't do it is we're overextended.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Ask the people in the Armed Forces today.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We've got Guards and Reserves who are doing double duties.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We've got a backdoor draft taking place in America today, people with stop-loss programs where they're told, "You can't get out of the military," 9 out of our 10 active duty divisions committed to Iraq one way or the other, either going, coming, or preparing.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: So this is the way the President has overextended the United States.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's why, in my plan, I add two active duty divisions to the United States Army, not for Iraq but for our general demands across the globe.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I also intend to double the number of Special Forces so that we can do the job we need to do with respect to fighting the terrorists around the world.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And if we do that, then we have the ability to be able to respond more rapidly.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But I'll tell you this, as President, if it took American forces, to some degree, to coalesce the African Union, I'd be prepared to do it, because we could never allow another Rwanda.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It's a moral responsibility for us in the world.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Back to Iran, just for a second.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It was not my administration that put the sanctions on Iran.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That happened long before I arrived in Washington, DC.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: In terms of Darfur, I agree, it's genocide, and Colin Powell so stated.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We have committed $200 million worth of aid.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're the leading donor in the world to help the suffering people there.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We will commit more, over time, to help.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We were very much involved at the U.N.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: on the sanction policy of the Bashir Government in the Sudan.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Prior to Darfur, Ambassador Jack Danforth had been negotiating a north-south agreement that we would hope would have brought peace to the Sudan.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I agree with my opponent that we shouldn't be committing troops, that we ought to be working with the African Union to do so—precisely what we did in Liberia.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We helped stabilize the situation with some troops, and when the African Union came, we moved them out.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My hope is that the African Union moves rapidly to help save lives.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Fortunately, the rainy season will be ending shortly, which will make it easier to get aid there and help the long-suffering people there.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Whew, that's a loaded question.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: First of all, I admire Senator Kerry's service to our country.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I admire the fact that he is a great dad.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I appreciate the fact that his daughters have been so kind to my daughters in what has been a pretty hard experience for, I guess, young girls seeing their dads out there campaigning.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I admire the fact that he's served for 20 years in the Senate, although I'm not so sure I admire the record.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I won't hold it against him that he went to Yale.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Nothing wrong with that.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I—my concerns about the Senator is that in the course of this campaign I've been listening very carefully to what he says, and he changed his positions on the war in Iraq, changed his positions on something as fundamental as what you believe in your core, in your heart of hearts, is right in Iraq.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You cannot lead if you send mixed messages.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Mixed messages send the wrong signals to our troops.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Mixed messages send the wrong signals to our allies.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Mixed messages send the wrong signals to the Iraqi citizens.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And that's my biggest concern about my opponent.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I admire his service.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But I just know how this world works and that in the councils of government, there must be certainty from the U.S.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: President.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Of course, we change tactics when need to, but we never change our beliefs, the strategic beliefs that are necessary to protect this country in the world.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, first of all, I appreciate enormously the personal comments the President just made, and I share them with him.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think only if you've—if you're doing this, and he's done it more than I have in terms of the Presidency, can you begin to get a sense of what it means to your families.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And it's tough.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And so I acknowledge his daughters.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've watched them.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've chuckled a few times at some of their comments.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And——

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I'm trying to put a leash on them.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, I know, I've learned not to do that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I have great respect and admiration for his wife.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think she's a terrific person——

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: ——and a great First Lady.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But we do have differences.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm not going to talk about a difference of character.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I don't think that's my job or my business.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But let me talk about something that the President just sort of finished up with—maybe someone would call it a character trait; maybe somebody wouldn't—but this issue of certainty.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It's one thing to be certain, but you can be certain and be wrong.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It's another to be certain and be right, or be certain and be moving in the right direction, or be certain about a principle and then learn new facts and take those new facts and put them to use in order to change and get your policy right.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: What I worry about with the President is that he's not acknowledging what's on the ground.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: He's not acknowledging the realities of North Korea.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: He's not acknowledging the truth of the science of stem cell research or of global warming and other issues.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And certainty sometimes can get you in trouble.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Well, I think—listen, I fully agree that one should shift tactics, and we will in Iraq.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Our commanders have got all the flexibility to do what is necessary to succeed.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But what I won't do is change my core values because of politics or because of pressure.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And it is—one of the things I've learned in the White House is that there's enormous pressure on the President, and you cannot wilt under that pressure.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Otherwise the world won't be better off.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I have no intention of wilting.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've never wilted in my life, and I've never wavered in my life.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I know exactly what we need to do in Iraq and my position has been consistent.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Saddam Hussein is a threat.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: He needed to be disarmed.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We needed to go to the U.N.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President needed the authority to use force in order to be able to get him to do something because he never did it without the threat of force, but we didn't need to rush to war without a plan to win the peace.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Nuclear proliferation— nuclear proliferation.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: There are some 600-plus tons of unsecured material still in the former Soviet Union, in Russia.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: At the rate that the President is currently securing that, it will take 13 years to get it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I did a lot of work on this.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I wrote a book about it several years ago—maybe 6 or 7 years ago, called "The New War," which saw the difficulties of this international criminal network.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And back then, we intercepted a suitcase in a Middle Eastern country with nuclear materials in it, and the black market sale price was about $250 million.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, there are terrorists trying to get their hands on that stuff today.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And this President, I regret to say, has secured less nuclear material in the last 2 years since 9/11 than we did in the 2 years preceding 9/11.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We have to do this job.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And to do the job, you can't cut the money for it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President actually cut the money for it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You have to put the money into it and the funding and the leadership.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And part of that leadership is sending the right message to places like North Korea.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Right now the President is spending hundreds of millions of dollars to research bunker-busting nuclear weapons.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The United States is pursuing a new set of nuclear weapons.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It doesn't make sense.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You talk about mixed messages.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We're telling other people, "You can't have nuclear weapons," but we're pursuing a new nuclear weapon that we might even contemplate using.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Not this President.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm going to shut that program down, and we're going to make it clear to the world we're serious about containing nuclear proliferation.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And we're going to get the job of containing all of that nuclear material in Russia done in 4 years.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And we're going to build the strongest international network to prevent nuclear proliferation.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This is the scale of what President Kennedy set out to do with the Nuclear Test Ban Treaty.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It's our generation's equivalent, and I intend to get it done.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Actually, we've increased funding for dealing with nuclear proliferation about 35 percent since I've been the President.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Secondly, we've set up what's called the—well, first of all, I agree with my opponent that the biggest threat facing this country is weapons of mass destruction in the hands of a terrorist network.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And that's why we've put proliferation as the—one of the centerpieces of a multipronged strategy to make the country safer.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My administration started what is called the Proliferation Security Initiative, over 60 nations involved with disrupting the trans-shipment of information and/or weapons of mass destruction materials.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And we're— been effective.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We busted the A.Q.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Khan network.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: This was a proliferator out of Pakistan that was selling secrets to places like North Korea and Libya.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We convinced Libya to disarm.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It was an essential part of dealing with weapons of mass destruction and proliferation.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I'll tell you another way to help protect America in the long—in the long run is continue with missile defenses, and we've got a robust research and development program that has been ongoing during my administration.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We'll be implementing a missile defense system relatively quickly.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And that is another way to help deal with the threats that we face in the 21st century.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent is opposed to the missile defenses.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: In the hands of a terrorist enemy.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Weapons of mass destruction, nuclear proliferation.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But again, the test of the difference between us—the President has had 4 years to try to do something about it, and North Korea has got more weapons.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Iran is moving towards weapons.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And at his pace, it will take 13 years to secure those weapons in Russia.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm going to do it in 4 years, and I'm going to immediately set out to have bilateral talks with North Korea.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Again, I can't tell you how big a mistake I think that is, to have bilateral talks with North Korea.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's precisely what Kim Chong-il wants.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It will cause the six-party talks to evaporate.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It means that China no longer is involved in convincing, along with us, for Kim Chong-il to get rid of his weapons.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's a big mistake to do that.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We must have China's leverage on Kim Chong-il, besides ourselves.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And if you enter bilateral talks, they'll be happy to walk away from the table.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I don't think that will work.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: No, I don't think it's okay and said so publicly.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think that there needs to be checks and balances in a democracy and made that very clear—that by consolidating power in a central government, he's sending a signal to the Western world and the United States that—that perhaps he doesn't believe in checks and balances.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And I've told him that.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He's also a strong ally in the war on terror.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He is—listen, they went through a horrible situation in Beslan where these terrorists gunned down young school kids.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But it's the nature of the enemy, by the way.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's why we need to be firm and resolved in bringing them to justice.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's precisely what Vladimir Putin understands as well.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I've got a good relation with Vladimir, and it's important that we do have a good relation because that enables me to better comment to him and to—better to discuss with him some of the decisions he makes.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I found that in this world that it's important to establish good personal relationships with people so that when you have disagreements, you're able to disagree in a way that is effective.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so I've told him my opinion.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I look forward to discussing it more with him as time goes on.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Russia is a country in transition.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Vladimir is going to have to make some hard choices, and I think it's very important for the American President as well as other Western leaders to remind him of the great benefits of democracy, that democracy will best help the people realize their hopes and aspirations and dreams.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And I will continue working with him over the next 4 years.

sentence: And it sort of brought home the transition to democracy that Russia was trying to make.

sentence: Mr.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: President.

sentence: My fellow Americans, as I said at the very beginning of this debate, both President Bush and I love this country very much.

sentence: I know that for many of you sitting at home, parents of kids in Iraq, you want to know, who is the person who could be a Commander in Chief who can get your kids home and get the job done and win the peace?

sentence: And for all the rest of the parents in America who are wondering about their kids going to a school or anywhere else in the world, what kind of world they're going to grow up in, let me look you in the eye and say to you: I've defended this country as a young man in war, and I will defend it as President of the United States.

sentence: I believe we're strongest when we reach out and lead the world and build strong alliances.

sentence: I believe we can be successful.

sentence: And we need a fresh start, a new credibility, a President who can bring allies to our side.

sentence: I also have a plan to win the war on terror, funding homeland security, strengthening our military, cutting off finances, reaching out to the world—again, building strong alliances.

sentence: I believe America's best days are ahead of us because I believe that the future belongs to freedom, not to fear.

sentence: That's the country that I'm going to fight for, and I ask you to give me the opportunity to make you proud.

sentence: I ask you to give me the opportunity to lead this great Nation so that we can be stronger here at home, respected again in the world, and have responsible leadership that we deserve.

sentence: If America shows uncertainty or weakness in this decade, the world will drift toward tragedy.

sentence: By being steadfast and resolute and strong, by keeping our word, by supporting our troops, we can achieve the peace we all want.

sentence: I appreciate your listening tonight.

sentence: And may God continue to bless our great land.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Gwen, I want to thank you, and I want to thank the folks here at Case Western Reserve for hosting this tonight.

sentence: It's a very important event, and they've done a superb job of putting it together.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: It's important to look at all of our developments in Iraq within the broader context of the global war on terror.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And, after 9/11, it became clear that we had to do several things to have a successful strategy to win the global war on terror, specifically that we had to go after the terrorists where ever we might find them, that we also had to go after state sponsors of terror, those who might provide sanctuary or safe harbor for terror.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And we also then finally had to stand up democracies in their stead afterwards, because that was the only way to guarantee that these states would not again become safe harbors for terror or for the development of deadly weapons.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Concern about Iraq specifically focused on the fact that Saddam Hussein had been, for years, listed on the state sponsor of terror, that they he had established relationships with Abu Nidal, who operated out of Baghdad; he paid $25,000 to the families of suicide bombers; and he had an established relationship with Al Qaida.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Specifically, look at George Tenet, the CIA director's testimony before the Committee on Foreign Relations two years ago when he talked about a 10-year relationship.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: The effort that we've mounted with respect to Iraq focused specifically on the possibility that this was the most likely nexus between the terrorists and weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: The biggest threat we faced today is the possibility of terrorists smuggling a nuclear weapon or a biological agent into one of our own cities and threatening the lives of hundreds of thousands of Americans.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: What we did in Iraq was exactly the right thing to do.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: If I had it to recommend all over again, I would recommend exactly the same course of action.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: The world is far safer today because Saddam Hussein is in jail, his government is no longer in power.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And we did exactly the right thing.

sentence: Vice President, you are still not being straight with the American people.

sentence: I mean, the reality you and George Bush continue to tell people, first, that things are going well in Iraq -- the American people don't need us to explain this to them, they see it on their television every single day.

sentence: We lost more troops in September than we lost in August; lost more in August than we lost in July; lost more in July than we lost in June.

sentence: And it's not just me that sees the mess in Iraq.

sentence: The notion of additional troops is talked about frequently, but the point of success in Iraq will be reached when we have turned governance over to the Iraqi people; they have been able to establish a democratic government.

sentence: They will have free elections next January for the first time in history.

sentence: We also are actively, rapidly training Iraqis to take on the security responsibility.

sentence: Those two steps are crucial to success in Iraq.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: They're well in hand, well under way.

sentence: And I'm confident that, in fact, we'll get the job done.

sentence: Vice President, there is no connection between the attacks of September 11th and Saddam Hussein.

sentence: And in fact the CIA is now about to report that the connection between Al Qaida and Saddam Hussein is tenuous at best.

sentence: And, in fact, the secretary of defense said yesterday that he knows of no hard evidence of the connection.

sentence: We need to be straight with the American people.

sentence: And doing it the right way meant that we were prepared; that we gave the weapons inspectors time to find out what we now know, that in fact there were no weapons of mass destruction; that we didn't take our eye off the ball, which are Al Qaida, Osama bin Laden, the people who attacked us on September the 11th.

sentence: Now, remember, we went into Afghanistan, which, by the way, was the right thing to do.

sentence: But we had Osama bin Laden cornered at Tora Bora.

sentence: We turned -- this is the man who masterminded the greatest mass murder and terrorist attack in American history.

sentence: They gave the responsibility of capturing and/or killing Saddam -- I mean Osama bin Laden to Afghan warlords who, just a few weeks before, had been working with Osama bin Laden.

sentence: We went into Afghanistan and very quickly the administration made a decision to divert attention from that and instead began to plan for the invasion of Iraq.

sentence: And these connections -- I want the American people to hear this very clearly.

sentence: Because there is no connection between Saddam Hussein and the attacks of September 11th -- period.

sentence: The senator has got his facts wrong.

sentence: I have not suggested there's a connection between Iraq and 9/11, but there's clearly an established Iraqi track record with terror.

sentence: And the point is that that's the place where you're most likely to see the terrorists come together with weapons of mass destruction, the deadly technologies that Saddam Hussein had developed and used over the years.

sentence: Now, the fact of the matter is, the big difference here, Gwen, is they are not prepared to deal with states that sponsor terror.

sentence: And they give absolutely no indication, based on that record, of being wiling to go forward and aggressively pursue the war on terror with a kind of strategy that will work, that will defeat our enemies and will guarantee that the United States doesn't again get attacked by the likes of Al Qaida.

sentence: Gwen, we've never let up on Osama bin Laden from day one.

sentence: We've captured or killed thousands of Al Qaida in various places around the world and especially in Afghanistan.

sentence: We'll continue to very aggressively pursue him, and I'm confident eventually we'll get him.

sentence: The key to success in Afghanistan has been, again, to go in and go after the terrorists, which we've done, and also take down the Taliban regime which allowed them to function there, in effect sponsors, if you will, of the Al Qaida organization.

sentence: John Edwards, two and a half years ago, six months after we went into Afghanistan announced that it was chaotic, the situation was deteriorating, the warlords were about to take over.

sentence: Here we are, two and a half years later, we're four days away from a democratic election, the first one in history in Afghanistan.

sentence: We've got 10 million voters who have registered to vote, nearly half of them women.

sentence: That election will put in place a democratically elected government that will take over next December.

sentence: We've made enormous progress in Afghanistan, in exactly the right direction, in spite of what John Edwards said two and a half years ago.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: He just got it wrong.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: The fact is, as we go forward in Afghanistan, we will pursue Osama bin Laden and the terrorists as long as necessary.

sentence: We're standing up Afghan security forces so they can take on responsibility for their own security.

sentence: We'll keep U.S.

sentence: forces there -- we have about 16,000 there today -- as long as necessary, to assist the Afghans in terms of dealing with their security situation.

sentence: When we had Osama bin Laden cornered, they left the job to the Afghan warlords.

sentence: Now, I want to go back to something the vice president said just a minute ago, because these distortions are continuing.

sentence: He said that -- made mention of this global test.

sentence: What John Kerry said -- and it's just as clear as day to anybody who was listening -- he said: We will find terrorists where they are and kill them before they ever do harm to the American people, first.

sentence: He defended this country as a young man, he will defend this country as president of the United States.

sentence: Not only are they providing 75 percent of the world's opium, large-cut parts of the country are under the control of drug lords and warlords.

sentence: Big parts of the country are still insecure.

sentence: And the reality is the part of Afghanistan, eastern Afghanistan, where Osama bin Laden is, is one of the hardest places to control and the most insecure, Gwen.

sentence: Twenty years ago we had a similar situation in El Salvador.

sentence: We had -- guerrilla insurgency controlled roughly a third of the country, 75,000 people dead, and we held free elections.

sentence: I was there as an observer on behalf of the Congress.

sentence: The human drive for freedom, the determination of these people to vote, was unbelievable.

sentence: And the terrorists would come in and shoot up polling places; as soon as they left, the voters would come back and get in line and would not be denied the right to vote.

sentence: And today El Salvador is a whale of a lot better because we held free elections.

sentence: The power of that concept is enormous.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And it will apply in Afghanistan, and it will apply as well in Iraq.

sentence: The vice president just said that we should focus on state sponsors of terrorism.

sentence: Iran has moved forward with its nuclear weapons program.

sentence: Well, let me say, first, he said in the same segment -- I don't remember precisely where it was connected with what you just read -- but he said, point blank, "We will never give anyone a veto over the security of the United States of America." sentence: First, we're going to actually tell the American people the truth.

sentence: We're not going to suggest to them that things are going well in Iraq or anyplace else when, in fact, they're not.

sentence: We're going to make sure that the American people know the truth about why we are using force and what the explanation for it is.

sentence: We're also going to make sure that we tell the world the truth.

sentence: Because the reality is, for America to lead, for America to do what it's done for 50 years before this president and vice president came into office, it is critical that we be credible.

sentence: It is critical that they believe that when America takes action, they can trust what we're doing, what we say, what we say at the United Nations, what we say in direct conversations with leaders of the world -- of other countries.

sentence: They need to know that the credibility of the United States is always good, because they will not follow us without that.

sentence: We will not outsource our responsibility to keep this country safe.

sentence: You also have a situation where you talk about credibility.

sentence: They don't need the vice president or the president to tell them what they saw.
