sentence: They saw a man who was strong, who had conviction, who is resolute, who made it very clear that he will do everything that has to be done to find terrorists, to keep the American people safe.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: He laid out his plan for success in Iraq, made it clear that we were committed to success in Iraq.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We have to be, because we have troops on the ground there and because they have created a haven for terrorists.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Your rhetoric, Senator, would be a lot more credible if there was a record to back it up.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: There isn't.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And you cannot use "talk tough" during the course of a 90-minute debate in a presidential campaign to obscure a 30-year record in the United States Senate and, prior to that by John Kerry, who has consistently come down on the wrong side of all the major defense issues that he's faced as a public official.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: I'm saying specifically that I don't believe he has the qualities we need in a commander in chief because I don't think, based on his record, that he would pursue the kind of aggressive policies that need to be pursued if we're going to defeat these terrorists.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We need to battle them overseas so we don't have to battle them here at home.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: I'm not challenging John Kerry's patriotism.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: I said in my acceptance speech in New York City at the Republican convention that we respected his service in Vietnam, and I got applause for that.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We've never criticized his patriotism.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: What we've questioned is his judgment.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And his judgment's flawed, and the record's there for anybody who wants to look at it.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: In 1984, when he ran for the Senate he opposed, or called for the elimination of a great many major weapons systems that were crucial to winning the Cold War and are important today to our overall forces.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: When Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait and occupied it in 1990 and '91, he stood up on the floor of the Senate and voted against going in to liberate Kuwait and push Saddam Hussein back to Iraq.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: The problem we have is that, if you look at his record, he doesn't display the qualities of somebody who has conviction.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And with respect to this particular operation, we've seen a situation in which, first, they voted to commit the troops, to send them to war, John Edwards and John Kerry, then they came back and when the question was whether or not you provide them with the resources they needed -- body armor, spare parts, ammunition -- they voted against it.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: I couldn't figure out why that happened initially.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And then I looked and figured out that what was happening was Howard Dean was making major progress in the Democratic primaries, running away with the primaries based on an anti-war record.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: So they, in effect, decided they would cast an anti-war vote and they voted against the troops.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Now if they couldn't stand up to the pressures that Howard Dean represented, how can we expect them to stand up to Al Qaida?

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: One thing that's very clear is that a long resume does not equal good judgment.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: I mean, we've seen over and over and over the misjudgments made by this administration.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: I want to go back to what the vice president just said, because it's a continuation of the things he's been doing, unfortunately, on the campaign trail; it's a continuation of what he began his first answer with tonight.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: John Kerry has voted for the biggest military appropriations bill in the country's history.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: John Kerry has voted for the biggest intelligence appropriations in the country's history.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: This vice president, when he was secretary of defense, cut over 80 weapons systems, including the very ones he's criticizing John Kerry for voting against.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: These are weapons systems, a big chunk of which, the vice president himself suggested we get rid of after the Cold War.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: The reality is that John Kerry has consistently supported the very men that he served with in Vietnam and led.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: On the $87 billion, it was clear at the time of that vote that they had no plan to win the peace.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We're seeing the consequences of that everyday on the ground right now.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We stood up and said: For our troops, we must have a plan to win the peace.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We also thought it was wrong to have a $20 billion fund out of which $7.5 billion was going to go to a no-bid contract for Halliburton, the vice president's former company.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: It was wrong then.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: It's wrong now.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Well, Gwen, I think the record speaks for itself.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: These are two individuals who have been for the war when the headlines were good and against it when their poll ratings were bad.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We have not seen the kind of consistency that a commander in chief has to have in order to be a leader in wartime and in order to be able to see the strategy through to victory.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: If we want to win the war on terror, it seems to me it's pretty clear the choice is George Bush, not John Kerry.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: John Kerry has been absolutely clear and consistent from the beginning that we must stay focused on the people who attacked us; that Saddam Hussein was a threat that needed to be addressed directly; that the weapons inspectors needed to have time to do their job.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Had they had time to do their job, they would have discovered what we now know, that in fact Saddam Hussein had no weapons, that in fact Saddam Hussein has no connection with 9/11, that in fact Saddam Hussein has little or no connection with Al Qaida.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Well, let's start with what we know.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: What we know is that the president and the vice president have not done the work to build the coalition that we need -- dramatically different than the first Gulf War.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We know that they haven't done it, and we know they can't do it.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They didn't, by the way, just reject the allies going into lead- up to the war.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They also rejected them in the effort to do the reconstruction in Iraq, and that has consequences.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: What we believe is, as part of our entire plan for Iraq -- and we have a plan for Iraq.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They have a plan for Iraq too: more of the same.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We have a plan for success.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: And that plan includes speeding up the training of the military.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We have less than half of the staff that we need there to complete that training.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Second, make sure that the reconstruction is sped up in a way that the Iraqis see some tangible benefit for what's happening.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: And by the way, if we need to, we can take Iraqis out of Iraq to train them.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: It is not secure enough.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: It's so dangerous on the ground that they can't be trained there.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We can take them out of Iraq for purposes of training.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We should do whatever has to be done to train the Iraqis and to speed up that process.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: That works in conjunction with making sure the elections take place on time.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Right now, the United Nations, which is responsible for the elections in January, has about 35 people there.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Now, that's compared with a much smaller country like East Timor, where they had over 200 people on the ground.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: You need more than 35 people to hold an election in Cleveland, much less in Iraq.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: And they keep saying the election's on schedule, this is going to happen.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: The reality is we need a new president with credibility with the rest of the world and who has a real plan for success.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Success breeds contribution, breeds joining the coalition.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Not only that, I want to go back to what the vice president said.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: He attacks us about the troops.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They sent 40,000 American troops into Iraq without the body armor they needed.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They sent them without the armored vehicles they needed.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: While they were on the ground fighting, they lobbied the Congress to cut their combat pay.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: This is the height of hypocrisy.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Well, Gwen, it's hard to know where to start; there are so many inaccuracies there.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: The fact of the matter is the troops wouldn't have what they have today if you guys had had your way.

sentence: You talk about internationalizing the effort.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: They don't have a plan.

sentence: Basically, it's an echo.

sentence: You made the comment that the Gulf War coalition in '91 was far stronger than this.

sentence: No.

sentence: We had 34 countries then; we've got 30 today.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We've got troops beside us.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: It's hard, after John Kerry referred to our allies as a coalition of the coerced and the bribed, to go out and persuade people to send troops and to participate in this process.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: You end up with a situation in which -- talk about demeaning.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: In effect, you demean the sacrifice of our allies when you say it's the wrong war, wrong place, wrong time, and oh, by the way, send troops.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Makes no sense at all.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: It's totally inconsistent.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: There isn't a plan there.

sentence: Our most important ally in the war on terror, in Iraq specifically, is Prime Minister Allawi.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: He came recently and addressed a joint session of Congress that I presided over with the speaker of the House.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And John Kerry rushed out immediately after his speech was over with, where he came and he thanked America for our contributions and our sacrifice and pledged to hold those elections in January, went out and demeaned him, criticized him, challenged his credibility.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: That is not the way to win friends and allies.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: You're never going to add to the coalition with that kind of attitude.

sentence: IFILL: Senator Edwards, 30 seconds.

sentence: The vice president suggests that we have the same number of countries involved now that we had in the first Gulf War.

sentence: The first Gulf War cost the American people $5 billion.

sentence: And regardless of what the vice president says, we're at $200 billion and counting.

sentence: Not only that, 90 percent of the coalition casualties, Mr.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Vice President, the coalition casualties, are American casualties.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Ninety percent of the cost of this effort are being borne by American taxpayers.

sentence: It is the direct result of the failures of this administration.

sentence: Classic example.

sentence: He won't count the sacrifice and the contribution of Iraqi allies.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: It's their country.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: They're in the fight.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: They're increasingly the ones out there putting their necks on the line to take back their country from the terrorists and the old regime elements that are still left.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: They're doing a superb job.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And for you to demean their sacrifices strikes me as...

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Oh, I'm not...

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: as beyond...

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: I'm not demeaning...

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: It is indeed.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: You suggested...

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: No, sir, I did not...

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: somehow they shouldn't count, because you want to be able to say that the Americans are taking 90 percent of the sacrifice.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: You cannot succeed in this effort if you're not willing to recognize the enormous contribution the Iraqis are increasingly making to their own future.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We'll win when they take on responsibility for governance, which they're doing, and when the take on responsibility for their own security, which they increasingly are doing.

sentence: Thanks.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Well, let me speak, first of all, to what the vice president just said, and then I'll answer that question.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: This, unfortunately -- what the vice president is telling people is inconsistent with everything they see every single day.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: It's a continuation of, "Well, there's a strong connection between Al Qaida and Saddam Hussein." It's not true.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: It's a continuation of at least insinuating that there's some connection between 9/11 and Saddam Hussein.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: It's not true.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: It's saying to the American people, as the president said last Thursday, and the vice president continues to say tonight, that things are going well in Iraq, contrary to what people who have been there have seen, including Republican leaders, contrary to what everyone in America sees on their television every day -- Americans being kidnapped, people being beheaded, parts of the country under the control of insurgents, even today, under the control of the insurgents.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: The vice president has still not said anything about what Mr.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Bremer said, about the failure to have adequate troops, the failure to be able to secure the country in the short term.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: You know, remember "shock and awe"?

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Look at where we are now.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: It is a direct result of the failure to plan, the failure to have others involved in this effort.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: This is not an accident.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Now, let me go back to your question.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: If we want to do the things that need to be done to keep this country safe, we can't be dragged kicking and screaming to it.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: One thing that everybody does agree on is that 9/11 did change things.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: But what's happened is this administration opposed the creation of a 9/11 Commission to find out why it happened and what we needed to do.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They opposed the creation of a Department of Homeland Security, and then they were for it.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We can't react that way.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We must be more aggressive.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: With John Kerry as president of the United States, we are committed to immediately implementing all of the reforms suggested by the 9/11 Commission, so that we have the information we need to find terrorists and crush them before hey hurt us.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: No, I do not.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And, Gwen, at the time, I was talking specifically about this question of unilateral sanctions.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: What happens when we impose unilateral sanctions is, unless there's a collective effort, then other people move in and take advantage of the situation and you don't have any impact, except to penalize American companies.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We've got sanctions on Iran now.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We may well want to go to the U.N.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Security Council and ask for even tougher sanctions if they don't live up to their obligations under the initial -- International Atomic Energy Agency Non-Proliferation Treaty.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We dealt with Iran differently than we have Iraq partly because Iran has not yet, as Iraq did, violated 12 years of resolutions by the U.N.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Security Council.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We're working with the Brits and the Germans and the French, who've been negotiating with the Iranians.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We recently were actively involved in a meeting with the board of governors in the International Atomic Energy Agency.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And as I say, there will be a follow-up meeting in November to determine whether or not Iran's living up to their commitments and obligations.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And if they aren't, my guess is then the board of governors will recommend sending the whole matter to the U.N.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Security Council for the application of the international sanctions, which I think would be exactly the right way to go.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We're addressing North Korea on a similar basis, working with the Chinese, the South Koreans, the Japanese and others to try to bring them around.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: One of the great by-products, for example, of what we did in Iraq and Afghanistan is that five days after we captured Saddam Hussein, Moammar Gadhafi in Libya came forward and announced that he was going to surrender all of his nuclear materials to the United States, which he has done.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: This was one of the biggest sources of proliferation in the world today in terms of the threat that was represented by that.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: The suppliers network that provided that, headed by Mr.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: A.Q.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Khan, has been shut down.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We've made major progress in dealing here with a major issue with respect to nuclear proliferation.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And we'll continue to press very hard on the North Koreans and the Iranians as well.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Well, the vice president talks about there being a member, or someone associated with Al Qaida, in Iraq.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: There are 60 countries who have members of Al Qaida in them.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: How many of those countries are we going to invade?

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Not only that, he talks about Iran.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: The reality about Iran is that Iran has moved forward with their nuclear weapons program on their watch.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They ceded responsibility to dealing with it to the Europeans.

sentence: Now, the vice president, as you pointed out, spoke out loudly for lifting the sanctions on Iraq.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: John Kerry and I believe we need to strengthen the sanctions on Iraq, including closing the loophole that allows companies to use a subsidiary, offshore subsidiaries to do business with Iran.

sentence: I mentioned Halliburton a few minute ago in connection with the $87 billion, and you raised it in this question.

sentence: This is relevant, because he was pushing for lifting sanctions when he was CEO of Halliburton.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Here's why we didn't think Halliburton should have a no-bid contract.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: While he was CEO of Halliburton, they paid millions of dollars in fines for providing false information on their company, just like Enron and Ken Lay.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They did business with Libya and Iran, two sworn enemies of the United States.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They're now under investigation for having bribed foreign officials during that period of time.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Not only that, they've gotten a $7.5 billion no-bid contract in Iraq, and instead of part of their money being withheld, which is the way it's normally done, because they're under investigation, they've continued to get their money.

sentence: I can respond, Gwen, but it's going to take more than 30 seconds.

sentence: Well, the reason they keep mentioning Halliburton is because they're trying to throw up a smokescreen.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: They know the charges are false.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: They know that if you go, for example, to factcheck.com , an independent Web site sponsored by the University of Pennsylvania, you can get the specific details with respect to Halliburton.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: It's an effort that they've made repeatedly to try to confuse the voters and to raise questions, but there's no substance to the charges.

sentence: These are the facts.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: The facts are the vice president's company that he was CEO of, that did business with sworn enemies of the United States, paid millions of dollars in fines for providing false financial information, it's under investigation for bribing foreign officials.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: The same company that got a $7.5 billion no-bid contract, the rule is that part of their money is supposed to be withheld when they're under investigation, as they are now, for having overcharged the American taxpayer, but they're getting every dime of their money.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: I'm happy to let voters make their own decision about this.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Well, first of all, I do agree that we've been largely absent, not entirely absent, but largely absent from the peace-making process over the last four years.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: And let me just say a couple of preliminary things and then talk about where we are now.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: First, the Israeli people not only have the right to defend themselves, they should defend themselves.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They have an obligation to defend themselves.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: I mean, if I can, just for a moment, tell you a personal story.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: I was in Jerusalem a couple of years ago, actually three years ago, in August of 2001, staying at the King David Hotel.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: We left in the morning, headed to the airport to leave, and later in the day I found out that that same day, not far from where we were staying, the Sbarro Pizzeria was hit by a suicide bomber in Jerusalem.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Fifteen people were killed.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Six children were killed.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: What are the Israeli people supposed to do?

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: How can they continue to watch Israeli children killed by suicide bombers, killed by terrorists?

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They have not only the right to the obligation to defend themselves.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Now, we know that the prime minister has made a decision, an historic decision, to unilaterally withdraw from Gaza.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: It's important for America to participate in helping with that process.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: Now, if Gaza's being used as a platform for attacking the Israeli people, that has to be stopped.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: And Israel has a right to defend itself.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They don't have a partner for peace right now.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: They certainly don't have a partner in Arafat, and they need a legitimate partner for peace.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: And I might add, it is very important for America to crack down on the Saudis who have not had a public prosecution for financing terrorism since 9/11.

speaker: EDWARDS
sentence: And it's important for America to confront the situation in Iran, because Iran is an enormous threat to Israel and to the Israeli people.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: Gwen, I want to go back to the last comment, and then I'll come back to Israel-Palestine.

sentence: The reason they keep trying to attack Halliburton is because they want to obscure their own record.

sentence: And Senator, frankly, you have a record in the Senate that's not very distinguished.

sentence: You've missed 33 out of 36 meetings in the Judiciary Committee, almost 70 percent of the meetings of the Intelligence Committee.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: You've missed a lot of key votes: on tax policy, on energy, on Medicare reform.

sentence: Your hometown newspaper has taken to calling you "Senator Gone." You've got one of the worst attendance records in the United States Senate.

sentence: Now, in my capacity as vice president, I am the president of Senate, the presiding officer.

sentence: In respect to Israel and Palestine, Gwen, the suicide bombers, in part, were generated by Saddam Hussein, who paid $25,000 to the families of suicide bombers.

sentence: We've been strong supporters of Israel.

sentence: The president stepped forward and put in place a policy basically that said we will support the establishment of two states.

sentence: First president ever to say we'll establish and support a Palestinian state nextdoor to Israelis.

sentence: But first, there has to be an interlocutor you can trust and deal with.

sentence: And we won't have that, we don't have it now, in a Yasser Arafat.

sentence: There has to be reform of the Palestinian system.

sentence: Well, Gwen, there are several things that I think need to be done and are being done.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We've, of course, been through a difficult recession, and then the aftermath of 9/11, where we lost over a million jobs after that attack.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: But we think the key is to address some basic, fundamental issues that the president's already working on.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: I think probably the most successful thing we can do with respect to ending poverty is to get people jobs.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: There's no better antidote to poverty than a good, well-paying job that allows somebody to take care of their own family.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: To do that, we have to make America the best place in the world to do business.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And that means we've got to deal effectively with tax policy.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We've got to reduce the litigation costs that are built into our society.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We've got to provide the adequate medical care and make certain that we can, in fact, create the opportunities that are vital to that process.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: I'd zero in, in particular, on education.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: I think the most important thing we can do is have a first-class public school system.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: I'm a product of public schools.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And the president, his first legislative priority was the No Child Left Behind Act.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: It was the first piece of legislation we introduced.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We got it passed that first summer on a bipartisan basis.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: We even had Ted Kennedy on board for the effort.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: And it does several things.

speaker: CHENEY
sentence: It establishes high standards.

speaker: CHENEY
