sentence: I also think we ought to continue to have good adoption law as an alternative to abortion.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And we need to promote maternity group homes, which my administration has done.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Culture of life is really important for a country to have if it's going to be a hospitable society.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, again, the President just said categorically, "My opponent is against this.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: My opponent is against that." It's just not that simple.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: No, I'm not.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm against the partial-birth abortion, but you've got to have an exception for the life of the mother and the health of the mother under the strictest test of bodily injury to the mother.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Secondly, with respect to parental notification, I'm not going to require a 16- or 17-year old kid who's been raped by her father and who's pregnant to have to notify her father.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: So you've got to have a judicial intervention.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And because they didn't have a judicial intervention where she could go somewhere and get help, I voted against it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It's never quite as simple as the President wants you to believe.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's pretty simple when they say, "Are you for a ban on partial-birth abortion?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Yes or no." And he was given a chance to vote, and he voted no.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And that's just the way it is.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's a vote.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It came right up.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's clear for everybody to see.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And as I said, you can run, but you can't hide.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's the reality.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Put a head fake on.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I have made a lot of decisions, some of them little, like appointments to a board you've never heard of, and some of them big.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And in a war, there's a lot of tactical decisions that historians will look back and say, "You shouldn't have done that.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You shouldn't have made that decision." And I'll take responsibility for them.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I'm human.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But on the big questions about whether or not we should have gone into Afghanistan, the big question about whether we should have removed somebody in Iraq, I'll stand by those decisions because I think they're right.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's really what you're— when they ask about the mistakes, that's what they're talking about.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: They're trying to say, "Did you make a mistake going into Iraq?" And the answer is absolutely not.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It was the right decision.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The Duelfer report confirmed that decision today, because what Saddam Hussein was doing was trying to get rid of sanctions so he could reconstitute a weapons program, and the biggest threat facing America is terrorists with weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We knew he hated us.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We knew he had been a—invaded other countries.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We knew he tortured his own people.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: On the tax cut, it's a big decision.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I did the right decision.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Our recession was one of the shallowest in modern history.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Now, you ask what mistakes—I made some mistakes in appointing people, but I'm not going to name them.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I don't want to hurt their feelings on national TV.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But history will look back, and I'm fully prepared to accept any mistakes that history judges to my administration.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Because the President makes the decisions, the President has to take the responsibility.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe the President made a huge mistake, a catastrophic mistake, not to live up to his own standard, which was build a true global coalition, give the inspectors time to finish their job, and go through the U.N.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: process to its end and go to war as a last resort.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I ask each of you just to look into your hearts, look into your guts—gut-check time.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Was this really going to war as a last resort?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President rushed our Nation to war without a plan to win the peace, and simple things weren't done.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's why Senator Lugar says "incompetent" in the delivery of services.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's why Senator Hagel, Republican, says, "beyond pitiful, beyond embarrassing, in the zone of dangerous." We didn't guard 850,000 tons of ammo.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That ammo is now being used against our kids.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Ten thousand out of twelve thousand Humvees aren't armored.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've visited some of those kids with no limbs today because they didn't have the armor on those vehicles.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They didn't have the right body armor.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've met parents who've, on the Internet, gotten the armor to send their kids.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: There's no bigger judgment for a President of the United States than how you take a nation to war.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And you can't say, "Because Saddam might have done it 10 years from now, that's a reason." That's an excuse.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He complains about the fact our troops don't have adequate equipment, yet he voted against the $87 billion supplemental I sent to the Congress and then issued one of the most amazing quotes in political history: "I actually did vote for the $87 billion, before I voted against it." Saddam Hussein was a risk to our country, ma'am.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And he was a risk that—and this is where we just have a difference of opinion.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The truth of the matter is, if you listen carefully: Saddam would still be in power if he were the President of the United States, and the world would be "a lot better off."

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Not necessarily be in power.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But here's what I'll say about the 87 billion: I made a mistake in the way I talked about it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: He made a mistake in invading Iraq.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Which is a worse decision?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, I voted the way I voted because I saw that he had the policy wrong, and I wanted accountability.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I didn't want to give a slush fund to Halliburton.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I also thought the wealthiest people in America ought to pay for it, ladies and gentlemen.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: He wants your kids to pay for it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I wanted us to pay for it, since we're at war.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I don't think that's a bad decision.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Go ahead.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Actually——

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You want to go first?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Either way.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Charlie, thank you.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And thank you all.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Thank you, all of you, for taking part; thanks for your questions tonight very, very much.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Obviously, the President and I both have very strong convictions.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I respect him for that, but we have a very different view about how to make America stronger and safer.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I will never cede the authority of our country or our security to any other nation.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'll never give a veto of American security to any other entity, not a nation, not a country, not an institution.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But I know, as I think you do, that our country is strongest when we lead the world, when we lead strong alliances.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And that's the way Eisenhower and Reagan and Kennedy and others did it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We are not doing that today.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We need to.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I have a plan that will help us go out and kill and find the terrorists, and I will not stop in our effort to hunt down and kill the terrorists.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But I also have a better plan on how we're going to deal with Iraq, training the Iraqi forces more rapidly, getting our allies back to the table with a fresh start, with new credibility, with a President whose judgment the rest of the world trusts.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: In addition to that, I believe we have a crisis here at home, a crisis of the middle class that is increasingly squeezed, health care costs going up.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I have a plan to provide health care to all Americans.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I have a plan to provide for our schools so we keep the standards, but we help our teachers teach and elevate our schools by funding No Child Left Behind.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I have a plan to protect the environment so that we leave this place in better shape to our children than we were handed it by our parents.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's the test.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe America's best days are ahead of us.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm an optimist.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But we have to make the right choices, to be fiscally responsible and to create the new jobs of the future.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We can do this.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I ask you for the privilege of leading our Nation to be stronger at home and respected again in the world.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Charlie, thanks.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Thank you all very much.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's been enjoyable.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The great contest for the Presidency is about the future, who can lead, who can get things done.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've been through a lot together as a country, been through a recession, corporate scandals, war.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And yet, think about where we are.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We added 1.9 million new jobs over the past 13 months.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The farm income in America is high.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Small businesses are flourishing.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Homeownership rate is at an alltime high in America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're on the move.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Tonight I had a chance to discuss with you what to do to keep this economy going: Keep the taxes low, don't increase the scope of the Federal Government, keep regulations down, legal reform, a health care policy that does not empower the Federal Government but empowers individuals, and an energy plan that will help us become less dependent on foreign sources of energy.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And abroad, we're at war, and it requires a President who is steadfast and strong and determined.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I vowed to the American people after that fateful day of September the 11th that we would not rest nor tire until we're safe.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The 9/11 Commission put out a report that said America is safer, but not yet safe.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: There's more work to be done.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We'll stay on the hunt on Al Qaida.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We'll deny sanctuary to these terrorists.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We'll make sure they do not end up with weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The great nexus, the great threat to our country is that these haters end up with weapons of mass destruction.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But our long-term security depends on our deep faith in liberty.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We'll continue to promote freedom around the world.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Freedom is on the march.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Tomorrow Afghanistan will be voting for a President.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: In Iraq, we'll be having free elections, and a free society will make this world more peaceful.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: God bless.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, first of all, Bob, thank you for moderating tonight.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Thank you, Arizona State, for welcoming us.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And thank you to the Presidential Commission for undertaking this enormous task.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We're proud to be here.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Mr.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: President, I'm glad to be here with you again to share similarities and differences with the American people.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Will we ever be safe and secure again?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Yes, we absolutely must be.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's the goal.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, how do we achieve it is the most critical component of it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe that this President, regrettably, rushed us into a war, made decisions about foreign policy, pushed alliances away, and as a result, America is now bearing this extraordinary burden where we are not as safe as we ought to be.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The measurement is not: Are we safer?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The measurement is: Are we as safe as we ought to be?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And there are a host of options that this President had available to him, like making sure that at all our ports in America, containers are inspected.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Only 95 percent of them—95 percent come in today uninspected.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's not good enough.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: People who fly on airplanes today—the cargo hold is not X-rayed, but the baggage is.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's not good enough.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Firehouses don't have enough firefighters in them.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Police officers are being cut from the streets of America because the President decided to cut the COPS program.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: So we can do a better job of homeland security.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I can do a better job of waging a smarter, more effective war on terror and guarantee that we go after the terrorists.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I will hunt them down, and we'll kill them.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We'll capture them.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We'll do what's ever necessary to be safe.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But I pledge this to you, America: I will do it in the way that Franklin Roosevelt and Ronald Reagan and John Kennedy and others did, where we build the strongest alliances, where the world joins together, where we have the best intelligence, and where we are able, ultimately, to be more safe and secure.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Bob, thank you very much.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I want to thank Arizona State as well.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Yes, we can be safe and secure if we stay on the offense against the terrorists and if we spread freedom and liberty around the world.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I have got a comprehensive strategy to not only chase down Al Qaida, wherever it exists—and we're making progress; three-quarters of Al Qaida leaders have been brought to justice—but to make sure that countries who harbor terrorists are held to account.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: As a result of securing ourselves and ridding the Taliban out of Afghanistan, the Afghan people had elections this weekend.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And the first voter was a 19-year-old woman.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Think about that.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Freedom is on the march.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We held to account a terrorist regime in Saddam Hussein.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: In other words, in order to make sure we're secure, there must be a comprehensive plan.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent, just this weekend, talked about how terrorism could be reduced to a "nuisance," comparing it to prostitution and illegal gambling.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think that attitude and that point of view is dangerous.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I don't think you can secure America for the long run if you don't have a comprehensive view as to how to defeat these people.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: At home, we'll do everything we can to protect the homeland.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I signed the homeland security bill to better align our assets and resources.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent voted against it.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're doing everything we can to protect our borders and ports.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But absolutely, we can be secure in the long run.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It just takes good, strong leadership.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Yes.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: When the President had an opportunity to capture or kill Usama bin Laden, he took his focus off of him, outsourced the job to Afghan warlords, and Usama bin Laden escaped.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Six months after he said, "Usama bin Laden must be caught, dead or alive," this President was asked, "Where is Usama bin Laden?" He said, "I don't know.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I don't really think about him very much.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm not that concerned." We need a President who stays deadly focused on the real war on terror.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Gosh, I don't think I ever said I'm not worried about Usama bin Laden.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's kind of one of those exaggerations.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Of course, we're worried about Usama bin Laden.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're on the hunt after Usama bin Laden.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're using every asset at our disposal to get Usama bin Laden.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent said this war is a matter of intelligence and law enforcement.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: No, this is a—war is a matter of using every asset at our disposal to keep the American people protected.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Bob, we relied upon a company out of England to provide about half of the flu vaccines for the United States citizen, and it turned out that the vaccine they were producing was contaminated.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so we took the right action and didn't allow contaminated medicine into our country.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're working with Canada to, hopefully—that they'll produce a—help us realize the vaccine necessary to make sure our citizens have got flu vaccinations during this upcoming season.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My call to our fellow Americans is, if you're healthy, if you're younger, don't get a flu shot this year.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Help us prioritize those who need to get the flu shot, the elderly and the young.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The CDC, responsible for health in the United States, is setting those priorities and is allocating the flu vaccine accordingly.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I haven't gotten a flu shot, and I don't intend to, because I want to make sure that those who are most vulnerable get treated.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We have a problem with litigation in the United States of America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Vaccine manufacturers are worried about getting sued, and so, therefore, they have backed off from providing this kind of vaccine.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: One of the reasons I'm such a strong believer in legal reform is so that people aren't afraid of producing a product that is necessary for the health of our citizens and then end up getting sued in a court of law.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But the best thing we can do now, Bob, given the circumstances with the company in England, is for those of us who are younger and healthy, don't get a flu shot.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This really underscores the problem with the American health care system.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It's not working for the American family, and it's gotten worse under President Bush over the course of the last years.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Five million Americans have lost their health insurance in this country.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You got about a million right here in Arizona—just shy, 950,000—who have no health insurance at all.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Eighty-two thousand Arizonians lost their health insurance under President Bush's watch.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Two hundred and twenty-three thousand kids in Arizona have no health insurance at all.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: All across our country—go to Ohio, 1.4 million Ohioans have no health insurance; 114,000 of them lost it under President Bush; Wisconsin, 82,000 Wisconsinites lost it under President Bush.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This President has turned his back on the wellness of America, and there is no system.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: In fact, it's starting to fall apart, not because of lawsuits—though they are a problem, and John Edwards and I are committed to fixing them—but because of the larger issue that we don't cover Americans.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Children across our country don't have health care.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We're the richest country on the face of the planet, the only industrialized nation in the world not to do it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I have a plan to cover all Americans.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We're going to make it affordable and accessible.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We're going to let everybody buy into the same health care plan the Senators and Congressmen give themselves.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I would, thank you.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I want to remind people listening tonight that a plan is not a litany of complaints, and a plan is not to lay out programs that you can't pay for.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He just said he wants everybody to be able to buy into the same plan that Senators and Congressman get.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That costs the Government $7,700 per family.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: If every family in America signed up like the Senator suggested, it would cost us $5 trillion over 10 years.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's an empty promise.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's called bait and switch.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Actually, it's not an empty promise.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It's really interesting because the President used that very plan as a reason for seniors to accept his prescription drug plan.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: He said, "If it's good enough for the Congressmen and Senators to have choice, seniors ought to have choice." What we do is we have choice.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I choose Blue Cross/Blue Shield.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Other Senators, other Congressman choose other programs.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But the fact is we're going to help Americans be able to buy into it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Those that can afford it are going to buy in themselves.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We're not giving this away for nothing.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'll tell you exactly how I can do it: by reinstating what President Bush took away, which is called pay as you go.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: During the 1990s, we had pay-as-you-go rules.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: If you were going to pass something in the Congress, you had to show where you were going to pay for it and how.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: President Bush has taken—he's the only President in history to do this.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: He's also the only President since—in 72 years to lose jobs, 1.6 million jobs lost.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: He's the only President to have incomes of families go down for the last 3 years, the only President to see exports go down, the only President to see the lowest level of business investment in our country as it is today.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, I'm going to reverse that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm going to change that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We're going to restore the fiscal discipline we had in the 1990s.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Every plan that I have laid out, my health care plan, my plan for education, my plan for kids to be able to get better college loans, I've shown exactly how I'm going to pay for those.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And we start—we don't do it exclusively, but we start by rolling back George Bush's unaffordable tax cut for the wealthiest people, people earning more than $200,000 a year, and we pass, hopefully, the McCain/Kerry commission, which identified some $60 billion that we can get.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We shut the loophole which has American workers actually subsidizing the loss of their own job.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They just passed an expansion of that loophole in the last few days, $43 billion of giveaways, including favors to the oil and gas industry and to people importing ceiling fans from China.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm going to stand up and fight for the American worker, and I'm going to do it in a way that's fiscally sound.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I show how I pay for the health care, how we pay for the education.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I have a manufacturing jobs credit.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We pay for it by shutting that loophole overseas.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We raise the student loans.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I pay for it by changing the relationship with the banks.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This President has never once vetoed one bill, the first President in 100 years not to do that.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Well, his rhetoric doesn't match his record.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He's been a Senator for 20 years.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He voted to increase taxes 98 times.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: When they tried to reduce taxes, he voted against that 127 times.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He talks about being a fiscal conservative or fiscally sound, but he voted over—he voted 277 times to waive the budget caps, which would have cost the taxpayers $4.2 trillion.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He talks about pay-go—I'll tell you what pay-go means when you're a Senator from Massachusetts, when you're a colleague of Ted Kennedy: Pay-go means you pay, and he goes ahead and spends.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He's proposed $2.2 trillion of new spending, and yet the so-called tax on the rich, which is also a tax on many small-business owners in America, raises 600 million by our account—billion—800 billion by his account.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: There is a tax gap.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And guess who usually ends up filling the tax gap?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The middle class.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I proposed a detailed budget, Bob.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I sent up my budget man to the Congress, and he says, "Here's how we're going to reduce the deficit in half by 5 years." It requires pro-growth policies that grow our economy and fiscal sanity in the Halls of Congress.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I say, Bob, "I've got policies to continue to grow our economy and create the jobs of the 21st century, and here's some help for you to go get an education.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Here's some help for you to go to a community college.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've expanded trade adjustment assistance.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We want to help pay for you to gain the skills necessary to fill the jobs of the 21st century." You know, there's a lot of talk about how to keep the economy growing, and we talk about fiscal matters.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But perhaps the best way to keep jobs here in America and to keep this economy growing is to make sure our education system works.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I went to Washington to solve problems.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And I saw a problem in the public education system in America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: They were just shuffling too many kids through the system, year after year, grade after grade, without learning the basics.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so we said, "Let's raise the standards.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're spending more money, but let's raise the standards and measure early and solve problems now, before it's too late." You know, education is how to help the person who has lost a job.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Education is how to make sure this—we've got a workforce that's productive and competitive.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You got—4 more years, I've got more to do to continue to raise standards, to continue to reward teachers and school districts that are working, to emphasize math and science in the classrooms, to continue to expand Pell grants, to make sure that people have an opportunity to start their career with a college diploma.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so to the person you talked to, I say, "Here's some help.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Here's some trade adjustment assistance money for you to go to a community college in your neighborhood, a community college which is providing the skills necessary to fill the jobs of the 21st century." And that's what we'd say to that person.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I want you to notice how the President switched away from jobs and started talking about education principally.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Let me come back in one moment to that, but I want to speak for a second, if I can, to what the President said about fiscal responsibility.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Being lectured by the President on fiscal responsibility is a little bit like Tony Soprano talking to me about law and order in this country.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This President has taken a $5.6 trillion surplus and turned it into deficits as far as the eye can see.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Health care costs for the average American have gone up 64 percent.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Tuitions have gone up 35 percent, gasoline prices up 30 percent.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Medicare premiums went up 17 percent a few days ago.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Prescription drugs are up 12 percent a year.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But guess what, America?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The wages of Americans have gone down.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The jobs that are being created in Arizona right now are paying about $13,700 less than the jobs that we're losing, and the President just walks on by this problem.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The fact is that he's cut job training money.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: A billion dollars was cut.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They only added a little bit back this year because it's an election year.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They've cut the Pell grants and the Perkins loans to help kids be able to go to college.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They've cut the training money.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They've wound up not even extending unemployment benefits and not even extending health care to those people who are unemployed.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm going to do those things because that's what right in America: Help workers to transition in every respect.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I don't blame them entirely for it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I blame the President for the things the President could do that has an impact on it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Outsourcing is going to happen.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've acknowledged that in union halls across the country.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've had shop stewards stand up and say, "Will you promise me you're going to stop all this outsourcing?" And I've looked them in the eye and I've said, "No, I can't do that." What I can promise you is that I will make the playing field as fair as possible, that I will, for instance, make certain that with respect to the tax system, that you as a worker in America are not subsidizing the loss of your job.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Today, if you're an American business, you actually get a benefit for going overseas.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You get to defer your taxes.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: So if you're looking at a competitive world, you say to yourself, "Hey, I do better overseas than I do here in America." That's not smart.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I don't want American workers subsidizing the loss of their own job.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And when I'm President, we're going to shut that loophole in a nanosecond, and we're going to use that money to lower corporate tax rates in America for all corporations 5 percent.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And we're going to have a manufacturing jobs credit and a job hiring credit so we actually help people be able to hire here.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The second thing that we can do is provide a fair trade playing field.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This President didn't stand up for Boeing when Airbus was violating international rules with subsidies.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: He discovered Boeing during the course of this campaign after I've been talking about it for months.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The fact is that the President had an opportunity to stand up and take on China for currency manipulation.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: There are companies that wanted to petition the administration.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They were told, "Don't even bother.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We're not going to listen to it." The fact is that there have been markets shut to us that we haven't stood up and fought for.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm going to fight for a fair trade playing field for the American worker.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I will fight for the American worker just as hard as I fight for my own job.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's what the American worker wants.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And if we do that, we can have an impact.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Plus, we need fiscal discipline.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Restore fiscal discipline, we'll do a lot better.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Whoo!

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Let me start with the Pell grants.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: In his last litany of misstatements, he said we cut Pell grants.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've increased Pell grants by a million students.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's a fact.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Here he talks to the workers; let me talk to the workers.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You got more money in your pocket as a result of the tax relief we passed and he opposed.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: If you have a child, you got a $1,000 child credit.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's money in your pocket.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: If you're married, we reduced the marriage penalty.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The code ought to encourage marriage, not discourage marriage.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We created a 10-percent bracket to help lower income Americans.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: A family of four making 40,000 received about $1,700 in tax relief.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's your money.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The way my opponent talks, he said we're going to spend the Government's money.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: No, we're spending your money.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And when you have more money in your pocket, you're able to better afford things you want.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I believe the role of Government is to stand side by side with our citizens to help them realize their dreams, not tell citizens how to live their lives.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent talks about fiscal sanity.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: His record in the United States Senate does not match his rhetoric.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He voted to increase taxes 98 times and to bust the budget 277 times.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Bob, anybody can play with these votes; everybody knows that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I have supported or voted for tax cuts over 600 times.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I broke with my party in order to balance the budget, and Ronald Reagan signed into law the tax cut that we voted for.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I voted for IRA tax cuts.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I voted for small-business tax cuts.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But you know why the Pell grants have gone up in their numbers?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Because more people qualified for them, because they don't have money.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But they're not getting the $5,100 the President promised them.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They're getting less money.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: There are more people who qualify.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's not what we want.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Senator, no one is playing with your votes.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You voted to increase taxes 98 times.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: When they voted—when they proposed reducing taxes, you voted against it 126 times.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You voted to violate the budget caps 277 times.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You know, there's a mainstream in American politics.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You sit right on the far left bank.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: As a matter of fact, your record is such that Ted Kennedy, your colleague, is the conservative Senator from Massachusetts.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You know, Bob, I don't know.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I just don't know.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I do know that we have a choice to make in America, and that is to treat people with tolerance and respect and dignity.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's important that we do that.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I also know, in a free society, people, consenting adults, can live the way they want to live.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And that's to be honored.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But as we respect someone's rights and as we profess tolerance, we shouldn't change—or have to change our basic views on the sanctity of marriage.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I believe in the sanctity of marriage.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think it's very important that we protect marriage as an institution between a man and a woman.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I proposed a constitutional amendment.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The reason I did so was because I was worried that activist judges are actually defining the definition of marriage.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And the surest way to protect marriage between a man and woman is to amend the Constitution.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It has also the benefit of allowing citizens to participate in the process.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: After all, when you amend the Constitution, State legislatures must participate in the ratification of the Constitution.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I'm deeply concerned that judges are making those decisions and not the citizenry of the United States.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You know, Congress passed a law called DOMA, the Defense of Marriage Act.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent was against it.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It basically protected States from the action of one State to another.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It also defined marriage as between a man and a woman.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But I'm concerned that that will get overturned, and if it gets overturned, then we'll end up with marriage being defined by courts.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And I don't think that's in our Nation's interest.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We're all God's children, Bob, and I think if you were to talk to Dick Cheney's daughter, who is a lesbian, she would tell you that she's being who she was.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: She's being who she was born as.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think if you talk to anybody, it's not choice.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've met people who've struggled with this for years, people who were in a marriage because they were living a sort of convention, and they struggled with it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I've met wives who are supportive of their husbands, or vice versa, when they finally sort of broke out and allowed themselves to live who they were, who they felt God had made them.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think we have to respect that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President and I share the belief that marriage is between a man and a woman.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe marriage is between a man and a woman.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But I also believe that because we are the United States of America, we're a country with a great, unbelievable Constitution, with rights that we afford people, that you can't discriminate in the workplace.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You can't discriminate in the rights that you afford people.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You can't disallow someone the right to visit their partner in a hospital.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You have to allow people to transfer property, which is why I'm for partnership rights and so forth.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, with respect to DOMA and the marriage laws, the States have always been able to manage those laws, and they're proving today, every State, that they can manage them adequately.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I respect their views.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I completely respect their views.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I am a Catholic, and I grew up learning how to respect those views.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But I disagree with them, as do many.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe that I can't legislate or transfer to another American citizen my article of faith.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: What is an article of faith for me is not something that I can legislate on somebody who doesn't share that article of faith.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe that choice is a woman's choice.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It's between a woman, God, and her doctor, and that's why I support that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, I will not allow somebody to come in and change Roe v.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Wade.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President has never said whether or not he would do that, but we know from the people he's tried to appoint to the court, he wants to.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I will not.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I will defend the right of Roe v.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Wade.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, with respect to religion, you know, as I said, I grew up a Catholic.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I was an altar boy.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I know that throughout my life, this has made a difference to me.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And as President Kennedy said when he ran for President, he said, "I'm not running to be a Catholic President.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I'm running to be a President who happens to be Catholic." Now, my faith affects everything that I do and choose.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: There's a great passage of the Bible that says, "What does it mean, my brother, to say you have faith, if there are no deeds?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Faith without works is dead." And I think that everything you do in public life has to be guided by your faith, affected by your faith, but without transferring it in any official way to other people.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's why I fight against poverty.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's why I fight to clean up the environment and protect this Earth.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's why I fight for equality and justice.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: All of those things come out of that fundamental teaching and belief of faith.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But I know this, that President Kennedy, in his Inaugural Address, told all of us that, "Here on Earth, God's work must truly be our own." And that's what we have to—so I think that's the test of public service.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think it's important to promote a culture of life.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think a hospitable society is a society where every being counts and every person matters.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I believe the ideal world is one in which every child is protected in law and welcomed to life.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I understand there's great differences on this issue of abortion, but I believe reasonable people can come together and put good law in place that will help reduce the number of abortions.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Take, for example, the ban on partial-birth abortion.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's a brutal practice.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: People from both political parties came together in the Halls of Congress and voted overwhelmingly to ban that practice.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It made a lot of sense.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent, in that he's out of the mainstream, voted against that law.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: What I'm saying is, is that as we promote life and promote a culture of life, surely there are ways we can work together to reduce the number of abortions: Continue to promote adoption laws—that's a great alternative to abortion; continue to fund and promote maternity group homes.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I will continue to promote abstinence programs.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: At the last debate, my opponent said his wife was involved with those programs.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's great, and I appreciate that very much.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: All of us ought to be involved with programs that provide a viable alternative to abortion.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Gosh, I sure hope it's not the administration.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: No, there is a—look, there's a systemic problem.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Health care costs are on the rise because the consumers are not involved in the decisionmaking process.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Most health care costs are covered by third parties, and therefore, the actual user of health care is not the purchaser of health care.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And there's no market forces involved with health care.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's one of the reasons I'm a strong believer in what they call health savings accounts.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: These are accounts that allow somebody to buy a low-premium, high-deductible catastrophic plan and couple it with tax-free savings.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Businesses can contribute; employees can contribute on a contractual basis.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But this is a way to make sure people are actually involved with the decisionmaking process on health care.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Secondly, I do believe the lawsuits—I don't believe, I know—that the lawsuits are causing health care costs to rise in America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's why I'm such a strong believer in medical liability reform.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: At the last debate, my opponent said, "Well, they only—these lawsuits only cause costs to go up by one percent." Well, he didn't include the defensive practice of medicine that costs the Federal Government some $28 billion a year and costs our society between 60 and 100 billion dollars a year.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Thirdly, one of the reasons why there's still high costs in medicine is because this is the—they don't use information technology.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's like if you looked at the—it's the equivalent of the buggy-and-horse days compared to other industries here in America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so we've got to introduce high technology into health care.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're beginning to do it.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're changing the language.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We want there to be electronic medical records to cut down on error as well as to reduce costs.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: People tell me that when the health care field is fully integrated with information technology, it will wring some 20 percent of the costs out of the system.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And finally, moving generic drugs to the market quicker.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: So, those are four ways to help control the costs in health care.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The reason health care costs are getting higher—one of the principal reasons is that this administration has stood in the way of commonsense efforts that would have reduced the costs.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Let me give you a prime example.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: In the Senate, we passed the right of Americans to import drugs from Canada.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But the President and his friends took it out in the House, and now you don't have that right.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President blocked you from the right to have less expensive drugs from Canada.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We also wanted Medicare to be able to negotiate bulk purchasing.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The VA does that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The VA provides lower cost drugs to our veterans.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We could have done that in Medicare.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Medicare is paid for by the American taxpayer.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Medicare belongs to you.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Medicare is for seniors who are— many of them—on fixed income, to lift them out of poverty.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But rather than help you, the taxpayer, have lower cost, rather than help seniors have less expensive drugs, the President made it illegal—illegal—for Medicare to actually go out and bargain for lower prices.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Result: $139 billion windfall profit to the drug companies coming out of your pockets.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's a large part of your 17-percent increase in Medicare premiums.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: When I'm President, I'm sending that back to Congress, and we're going to get a real prescription drug benefit.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, we also have people sicker because they don't have health insurance.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: So whether it's diabetes or cancer, they come to the hospitals later, and it costs America more.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We've got to have health care for all Americans.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think it's important, since he talked about the Medicare plan— he's been in the United States Senate for 20 years.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He has no record on reforming of health care, no record at all.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: He introduced some 300 bills, and he's passed 5— no record of leadership.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I came to Washington to solve problems.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I was deeply concerned about seniors having to choose between prescription drugs and food, and so I led.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And in 2006, our seniors will get a prescription drug coverage in Medicare.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Once again, the President is misleading America.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've actually passed 56 individual bills that I've personally written.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And in addition to that, they're not always under my name; there is amendments on certain bills.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But more importantly, with respect to the question of "no record," I helped write—I did write—I was one of the original authors of the early childhood health care and the expansion of health care that we did in the middle of the 1990s.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I'm very proud of that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: So the President's wrong.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's correct.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, two leading national news networks have both said the President's characterization of my health care plan is incorrect.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: One called it fiction.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The other called it untrue.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The fact is that my health care plan, America, is very simple.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It gives you the choice.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I don't force you to do anything.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It's not a Government plan.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The Government doesn't require you to do anything.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You choose your doctor.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You choose your plan.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: If you don't want to take the offer of the plan that I want to put forward, you don't have to.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You can keep what you have today, keep a high deductible, keep high premiums, keep a high co-pay, keep low benefits.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But I got a better plan, and I don't think a lot of people are going to want to keep what they have today.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Here's what I do.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We take over Medicaid children from the States so that every child in America is covered.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And in exchange, if the States want to—they're not forced to; they can choose to—they cover individuals up to 300 percent of poverty.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It's their choice.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think they'll choose it, because it's a net plus of $5 billion to them.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We allow you—if you choose to; you don't have to—but we give you broader competition to allow you to buy into the same health care plan that Senators and Congressmen give themselves.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: If it's good enough for us, it's good enough for every American.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe that your health care is just as important as any politician in Washington, DC.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: If you want to buy into it, you can.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We give you broader competition.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That helps lower prices.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: In addition to that, we're going to allow people 55 to 64 to buy into Medicare early.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And most importantly, we give small business a 50-percent tax credit so that after we lower the cost of health care, they also get, whether they're self-employed or a small business, a lower cost to be able to cover their employees.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, what happens is, when you begin to get people covered like that—for instance, in diabetes, if you diagnose diabetes early, you could save $50 billion in the health care system of America by avoiding surgery and dialysis.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It works, and I'm going to offer it to America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: In all due respect, I'm not so sure it's credible to quote leading news organizations about—well, never mind.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Anyway— —let me quote the Lewin report.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The Lewin report is a group of folks who are not politically affiliated.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: They analyzed the Senator's plan.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It costs $1.2 trillion.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The Lewin report accurately noted that there are going to be 20 million people—over 20 million people added to Government-controlled health care.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It will be the largest increase in Government health care ever.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: If you raise the Medicaid to 300 percent, it provides an incentive for small businesses not to provide private insurance to their employees.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Why should they insure somebody when the Government is going to insure for them?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's estimated that 8 million people will go from private insurance to Government insurance.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We have a fundamental difference of opinion.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think Government-run health will lead to poor quality health, will lead to rationing, will lead to less choice.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Once a health care program ends up in a line item in the Federal Government budget, it leads to more controls.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And just look at other countries that have tried to have federally controlled health care.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: They have poor quality health care.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Our health care system is the envy of the world because we believe in making sure that the decisions are made by doctors and patients, not by officials in the Nation's Capital.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President just said that Government-run health care results in poor quality.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, maybe that explains why he hasn't fully funded the VA, and the VA hospital is having trouble, and veterans are complaining.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Maybe that explains why Medicare patients are complaining about being pushed off of Medicare—he doesn't adequately fund it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But let me just say to America, I am not proposing a Government-run program.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's not what I have.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I have Blue Cross/Blue Shield.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Senators and Congressmen have a wide choice.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Americans ought to have it too.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You talk about the VA.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've increased VA funding by 22 billion in the 4 years since I've been President.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's twice the amount that my predecessor increased VA funding.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Of course, we're meeting our obligation to our veterans, and the veterans know that.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're expanding veterans' health care throughout the country.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're aligning facilities where the veterans live now.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Veterans are getting very good health care under my administration, and they will continue to do so during the next 4 years.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Bob, first let me make sure that every senior listening today understands that when we're talking about reforming Social Security, that they'll still get their checks.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I remember the 2000 campaign; people said, "If George W.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: gets elected, your check will be taken away." Well, people got their checks, and they will continue to get their checks.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: There is a problem for our youngsters, a real problem, and if we don't act today, the problem will be valued in the trillions.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so I think we need to think differently.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We'll honor our commitment to our seniors, but for young—for our children and our grandchildren, we need to have a different strategy.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: In recognizing that, I called together a group of our fellow citizens to study the issue.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It was a committee chaired by the late Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York, a Democrat.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And they came up with a variety of ideas for people to look at.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I believe that younger workers ought to be allowed to take some of their own money and put it in a personal savings account, because I understand that they need to get better rates of return than the rates of return being given in the current Social Security trust.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And the compounding rate of interest effect will make it more likely that the Social Security system is solvent for our children and our grandchildren.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I will work with Republicans and Democrats.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: This will be a vital issue in my second term.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It is an issue that I'm willing to take on.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so I'll bring Republicans and Democrats together, and we're of course going to have to consider the costs.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But I want to warn my fellow citizens the cost of doing nothing, the cost of saying the current system is okay, far exceeds the cost of trying to make sure we save the system for our children.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: You just heard the President say that young people ought to be able to take money out of Social Security and put it in their own accounts.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, my fellow Americans, that's an invitation to disaster.

speaker: KERRY

sentence: I have a record of fighting for fiscal responsibility.

speaker: KERRY

sentence: If you take the tax cut that the President of the United States has given—President Bush gave to Americans in the top 1 percent of America, just that tax cut that went to the top 1 percent of America would have saved Social Security until the year 2075.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And when I roll it back and we invest in the things that I've talked about to move our economy, we're going to grow sufficiently that we begin to cut the deficit in half, and we get back to where we were at the end of the 1990s when we balanced the budget and paid down the debt of this country.

sentence: Now, if later on, after a period of time, we find that Social Security is in trouble, then we'll pull together the top experts of the country.

sentence: And so, in order to take pressure off the border, in order to make the borders more secure, I believe there ought to be a temporary-worker card that allows a willing worker and a willing employer to mate up—so long as there's not an American willing to do the job—to join up in order to be able to fulfill the employer's needs.

sentence: I think that it is a matter of fundamental right that if we raise the minimum wage, 15 million Americans would be positively affected.

sentence: But let me talk about what's really important for the worker you're referring to, and that's to make sure the education system works, is to make sure we raise standards.

sentence: We'll increase Federal spending, but in return for extra spending, we now want people to measure—States and local jurisdictions to measure, to show us whether or not a child can read or write or add and subtract." speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, I think the fact that they're facing these repeated callups, some of them two and three deployments, and there's a stop-loss policy that prevents people from being able to get out when their time was up, is a reflection of the bad judgment this President exercised in how he has engaged in the world and deployed our forces.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, I've proposed adding two active-duty divisions to the Armed Forces of the United States, one combat, one support.

sentence: In addition, I'm going to double the number of special forces so that we can fight a more effective war on terror with less pressure on the National Guard and Reserve.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And what I would like to do is see the National Guard and Reserve be deployed differently here in our own country.

sentence: There's much we can do with them with respect to homeland security.

sentence: But the most important thing to relieve the pressure on all of our Armed Forces is, frankly, to run a foreign policy that recognizes that America is strongest when we are working with real alliances, when we are sharing the burdens of the world by working through our statesmanship at the highest levels and our diplomacy to bring other nations to our side.

sentence: The fact is that he did not choose to go to war as a last resort.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And America now is paying already 120 billion, up to 200 billion before we're finished and much more, probably, and that is the result of this President taking his eye off of Usama bin Laden.

sentence: The best way to take the pressure off our troops is to succeed in Iraq, is to train Iraqis so they can do the hard work of democracy, is to give them a chance to defend their country, which is precisely what we're doing.

sentence: I did think we ought to extend the assault weapons ban and was told the fact that the bill was never going to move because Republicans and Democrats were against the assault weapon ban, people of both parties.
