sentence: We used to—we have a goal there for minority set-aside programs to try to encourage ownership in the country.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They don't reach those goals.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They don't even fight to reach those goals.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They've tried to undo them.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The fact is that in too many parts of our country, we still have discrimination, and affirmative action is not just something that applies to people of color.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Some people have a mistaken view of it in America.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It also is with respect to women.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: It's with respect to other efforts to try to reach out and be inclusive in our country.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think that we have a long way to go, regrettably.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: If you look at what's happened, we've made progress; I want to say that at the same time.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: During the Clinton years, as you may recall, there was a fight over affirmative action.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And there were many people, like myself, who opposed quotas, who felt there were places where it was overreaching.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: So we had a policy called "mend it, don't end it." We fixed it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And we fixed it for a reason, because there are too many people still in this country who feel the stark resistance of racism.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And so we have a distance to travel.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: As President, I will make certain we travel it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Now, let me just share something.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This President is the first President ever, I think, not to meet with the NAACP.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This is a President who hasn't met with the Black Congressional Caucus.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: This is a President who has not met with the civil rights leadership of our country.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: If a President doesn't reach out and bring people in and be inclusive, then how are we going to get over those barriers?

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I see that as part of my job as President, and I'll make my best effort to do it.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Well, first of all, it is just not true that I haven't met with the Black Congressional Caucus.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I met with the Black Congressional Caucus at the White House.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And secondly, like my opponent, I don't agree we ought to have quotas—I agree, we shouldn't have quotas.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But we ought to have an aggressive effort to make sure people are educated, to make sure when they get out of high school there's Pell grants available for them, which is what we've done.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've expanded Pell grants by a million students.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Do you realize, today in America, we spend $73 billion to help 10 million low- and middle-income families better afford college?

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's the access I believe is necessary, is to make sure every child learns to read, write, add, and subtract early, to be able to build on that education by going to college so they can start their careers with a college diploma.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I believe the best way to help our small businesses is not only through small-business loans, which we have increased since I've been the President of the United States, but to unbundle Government contracts so people will have a chance to be able to bid and receive a contract to help get their business going.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Minority ownership of businesses are up because we created an environment for the entrepreneurial spirit to be strong.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think—I believe part of a hopeful society is one in which somebody owns something.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Today in America more minorities own a home than ever before.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And that's hopeful, and that's positive.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: First, my faith plays a lot—a big part in my life.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And that's— when I was answering that question, what I was really saying to the person was that I pray a lot, and I do.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And my faith is a very—it's very personal.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I pray for strength.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I pray for wisdom.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I pray for our troops in harm's way.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I pray for my family.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I pray for my little girls.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But I'm mindful, in a free society, that people can worship if they want to or not.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You're equally an American if you choose to worship an Almighty and if you choose not to.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: If you're a Christian, Jew, or Muslim, you're equally an American.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's the great thing about America, is the right to worship the way you see fit.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Prayer and religion sustain me.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I've received calmness in the storms of the Presidency.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I love the fact that people pray for me and my family all around the country.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Somebody asked me one time, "Well, how do you know?" I said, "I just feel it." Religion is an important part.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I never want to impose my religion on anybody else, but when I make decisions, I stand on principle.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And the principles are derived from who I am.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I believe we ought to love our neighbor like we love ourself.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's manifested in public policy through the Faith-Based Initiative, where we've unleashed the armies of compassion to help seal—heal people who hurt.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I believe that God wants everybody to be free.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: That's what I believe.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And that's part of my foreign policy.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: In Afghanistan, I believe that the freedom there is a gift from the Almighty, and I can't tell you how encouraged I am to see freedom on the march.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And so my principles that I make decisions on are a part of me, and religion is a part of me.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, I respect everything that the President has said, and certainly I respect his faith.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think it's important, and I share it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think that he just said that freedom is a gift from the Almighty.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Everything is a gift from the Almighty.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And as I measure the words of the Bible—and we all do; different people measure different things, the Koran, the Torah, or— Native Americans who gave me a blessing the other day had their own special sense of connectedness to a higher being, and people all find their ways to express it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I was taught—I went to a church school, and I was taught that the two greatest commandments are "Love the Lord, your God, with all your mind, your body, and your soul" and "Love your neighbor as yourself." And frankly, I think we have a lot more loving of our neighbor to do in this country and on this planet.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We have a separate and unequal school system in the United States of America.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: There's one for the people who have, and there's one for the people who don't have.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And we're struggling with that today.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: The President and I have a difference of opinion about how we live out our sense of our faith.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I talked about it earlier when I talked about the works and faith without works being dead.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think we've got a lot more work to do.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And as President, I will always respect everybody's right to practice religion as they choose or not to practice, because that's part of America.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, very much so.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Let me pay a compliment to the President, if I may.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think in those days after 9/11, I thought the President did a terrific job.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I really was moved as well as impressed by the speech that he gave to the Congress.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I think the hug Tom Daschle gave him at that moment was about as genuine a sense of there being no Democrats, no Republicans; we were all just Americans.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's where we were.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: That's not where we are today.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I regret to say that the President, who called himself a uniter, not a divider, is now presiding over the most divided America in the recent memory of our country.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've never seen such ideological squabbles in the Congress of the United States.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've never seen members of a party locked out of meetings the way they're locked out today.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We have to change that, and as President, I am committed to changing that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I don't care if the idea comes from the other side or this side.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think we have to come together and work to change it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I've done that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Over 20 years in the United States Senate, I've worked with John McCain, who's sitting here.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've worked with other colleagues.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've reached across the aisle.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I've tried to find the common ground, because that's what makes us strong as Americans.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And if Americans trust me with the Presidency, I can pledge to you, we will have the most significant effort—openly, not secret meetings in the White House with special interests, not ideologically driven efforts to push people aside, but a genuine effort to try to restore America's hope and possibilities by bringing people together.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And one of the ways we're going to do it is, I'm going to work with my friend John McCain to further campaign finance reform so we get these incredible amounts of money out of the system and open it up to average people so America is really represented by the people who make up America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My biggest disappointment in Washington is how partisan the town is.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I had a record of working with Republicans and Democrats as the Governor of Texas, and I was hopeful to be able to do the same thing.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And we made good progress early on.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: The No Child Left Behind Act, incredibly enough, was good work between me and my administration and people like Senator Ted Kennedy.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And we worked together with Democrats to relieve the tax burden on the middle class and all who pay taxes in order to make sure this economy continues to grow.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But Washington is a tough town, and the way I view it is there's a lot of entrenched special interests there, people who are on one side of the issue or another, and they spend enormous sums of money, and they convince different Senators to tout their way or different Congressmen to talk about their issue, and they dig in.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I'll continue in the 4 years to continue to try to work to do so.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent said this is a bitterly divided time.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It was pretty divided in the 2000 election.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: So, in other words, it's pretty divided during the 1990s as well.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We're just in a period, and we've got to work to bring it out.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My opponent keeps mentioning John McCain, and I'm glad he did.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: John McCain is for me for President because he understands I have the right view in winning the war on terror and that my plan will succeed in Iraq, and my opponent has got a plan of retreat and defeat in Iraq.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: To listen to them— —to stand up straight and not scowl.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I love the strong women around me.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I can't tell you how much I love my wife and our daughters.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I am— you know, it's really interesting, I tell the people on the campaign trail, when I asked Laura to marry me, she said, "Fine, just so long as I never have to give a speech." I said, "Okay, you got a deal." Fortunately, she didn't hold me to that deal, and she's out campaigning, along with our girls, and she speaks English a lot better than I do.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think people understand what she's saying.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: But they see a compassionate, strong, great First Lady in Laura Bush.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I can't tell you how lucky I am when I met her in the backyard at Joe and Jan O'Neill in Midland, Texas.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It was the classic backyard barbecue.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: O'Neill said, "Come on over.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I think you'll find somebody who might interest you." So I said, "All right," popped over there.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: There was only four of us there, and not only did she interest me, I guess you could say it was love at first sight.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Well, I guess the President and you and I are three examples of lucky people who married up.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And some would say maybe me more so than others.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: But I can take it.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Can I say, if I could just say a word about a woman that you didn't ask about, but my mom passed away a couple years ago, just before I was deciding to run.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And she was in the hospital, and I went in to talk to her and tell her what I was thinking of doing.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And she looked at me from her hospital bed, and she just looked at me, and she said, "Remember, integrity, integrity, integrity." Those are the three words that she left me with.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And my daughters and my wife are people who just are filled with that sense of what's right, what's wrong.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They also kick me around.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They keep me honest.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They don't let me get away with anything.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I can sometimes take myself too seriously.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: They surely don't let me do that.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I'm blessed, as I think the President is blessed.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: As I said last time, I've watched him with the First Lady, who I admire a great deal, and his daughters—he's a great father.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I think we're both very lucky.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: My fellow Americans, as you heard from Bob Schieffer a moment ago, America is being tested by division.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: More than ever, we need to be united as a country.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And like Franklin Roosevelt, I don't care whether an idea is a Republican idea or a Democrat idea.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I just care whether it works for America and whether it's going to make us stronger.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: These are dangerous times.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe I offer tested, strong leadership that can calm the waters of a troubled world.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I believe that we can, together, do things that are within the grasp of Americans.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We can lift our schools up.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We can create jobs that pay more than the jobs we're losing overseas.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We can have health care for all Americans.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: We can further the cause of equality in our Nation.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Let me just make it clear: I will never allow any country to have a veto over our security.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Just as I fought for our country as a young man, with the same passion I will fight to defend this Nation that I love.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And with faith in God and with conviction in the mission of America, I believe that we can reach higher.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I believe we can do better.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I think the greatest possibilities of our country, our dreams and our hopes, are out there just waiting for us to grab onto them.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: And I ask you to embark on that journey with me.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I ask you for your trust.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I ask you for your help.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: I ask you to allow me the privilege of leading this great Nation of ours, of helping us to be stronger here at home and to be respected again in the world and, most of all, to be safer forever.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: KERRY
sentence: Good night, and God bless the United States of America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: In the Oval Office, there's a painting by a friend of Laura and mine named—by Tom Lea.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's a west Texas painting, a painting of a mountain scene.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And he said this about it, he said, "Sarah and I live on the east side of the mountain.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's the sunrise side, not the sunset side.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: It's the side to see the day that is coming, not to see the day that is gone." I love the optimism in that painting because that's how I feel about America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: You know, we've been through a lot together during the last 3 3/4 years.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've come through a recession, a stock market decline, an attack on our country.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And yet, because of the hard work of the American people and good policies, this economy is growing.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Over the next 4 years, we'll make sure the economy continues to grow.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We reformed our school system, and now there's an achievement gap in America that is beginning to close.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Over the next 4 years, we'll continue to insist on excellence in every classroom in America so that our children have a chance to realize the great promise of America.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Over the next 4 years, we'll continue to work to make sure health care is available and affordable.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: Over the next 4 years, we'll continue to rally the armies of compassion to help heal the hurt that exists in some of our country's neighborhoods.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I'm optimistic that we'll win the war on terror, but I understand it requires firm resolve and clear purpose.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We must never waver in the face of this enemy that—these ideologues of hate.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: And as we pursue the enemy wherever it exists, we'll also spread freedom and liberty.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: We've got great faith in the ability of liberty to transform societies, to convert hostile—a hostile world to a peaceful world.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: My hope for America is a prosperous America, a hopeful America, and a safer world.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I want to thank you for listening tonight.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: I'm asking for your vote.

speaker: BUSH
sentence: God bless you.
